FOREWORD







The authors navigate the connection between medicine and machine learning, unraveling the profound influence that machine learning has had on healthcare practices and patient care. They explain the integration of cutting-edge technologies that have become paramount in enhancing diagnostics, treatment, and patient outcomes. Among the groundbreaking innovations, machine learning has emerged as a transformative force, revolutionizing the way for medical predictions.

As we embark on this enlightening journey, readers will gain insights into the myriad applications of machine learning in predictive medicine. From early disease prediction with the help of machine learning, the impact is far-reaching and transformative. The relationship between data-driven algorithms and medical expertise has ushered in an era where predictive analytics not only assist clinicians in decision-making but also contribute to a more patient-centric and efficient healthcare ecosystem.

This content delves into the far-reaching applications of machine learning, from predictive diagnostics to treatment optimization, offering a panoramic view of its transformative influence on medical practices. By unraveling complex patterns and deciphering the intricate tapestry of patient data, machine learning not only augments the capabilities of healthcare professionals but propels us toward a future where proactive, personalized, and precise medicine is the norm. The compilation is not merely a testament to technological advancements; it is a celebration of the collaborative synergy between medical professionals, data scientists, and technologists. By embracing the potential of machine learning, authors pave the way for a future where healthcare is not only proactive but also increasingly precise and personalized.

I commend the contributors of authors for this volume for their insightful exploration of a topic that holds immense promise for the future of healthcare. Their collective expertise and dedication have illuminated the path towards a healthcare and machine learning integration that is not only more efficient but also inherently compassionate and patient-focused.

I extend my gratitude to the contributors of this work, whose dedication to unraveling the complexities of machine learning in medicine has resulted in a resource that will undoubtedly shape the discourse surrounding the future of healthcare.

Ajay Kumar
Director
Inderprastha Engineering College
AKTU University
U.P, India

PREFACE







The purpose of this book is to unravel the intricate threads that weave together the realms of machine learning and medical science. The content of this book aspires to be a guide through the intricate labyrinth of possibilities that machine learning presents in the field of medicine. In the dynamic landscape of modern healthcare, the intersection of medicine and technology has ushered in an era of unprecedented possibilities. The integration of machine learning, a subset of artificial intelligence, has emerged as a transformative force, reshaping the way we approach diagnosis, treatment, and patient care.

The book, "Prediction in Medicine: The Impact of Machine Learning on Healthcare," endeavors to navigate the intricate tapestry of advancements that this synergy has birthed. A journey is embarked through the various facets of predictive analytics, examining how machine learning algorithms are reshaping diagnostic paradigms, treatment strategies, and the overall patient experience. From the nuanced interpretation of medical imaging to the prediction of disease trajectories, the fusion of machine learning and healthcare is a narrative of innovation, precision, and ultimately improved patient outcomes. This book is not just a testament to the strides made in the field but also a guide for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers navigating this evolving landscape. It is an exploration of the promises and pitfalls, the breakthroughs and barriers that accompany the union of medicine and machine learning. On the precipice of a medical revolution, it becomes imperative to comprehend the profound implications of machine learning in the realm of healthcare. The content serves as a comprehensive exploration of how predictive analytics, driven by sophisticated algorithms and vast datasets, is becoming a linchpin in the decision-making processes of medical professionals, whether you are a healthcare professional seeking insights into the future of your field or a curious reader intrigued by the union of machine learning and medicine, which invites you to embark on a voyage of discovery. Striking a balance between technological advancement and ethical guidelines is paramount to ensure that these tools are wielded judiciously and for the betterment of patient outcomes.

As we embark on this intellectual journey, may this book serve as a compass, navigating the reader through the vast terrain of predictive medicine and offering insights into a future where data-driven decisions are synonymous with superior healthcare.

Predictive Analysis: Forecasting Patient's Outcomes and Medical Trends



Alka Singhal1, *, Dhanalekshmi Gopinathan1
1 Jaypee Institute of Information Technology, Uttar Pradesh, India

Abstract

Predictive analysis is rapidly transforming the healthcare industry by leveraging advanced data analytics techniques to predict patient outcomes and identify medical record trends. With the increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs), wearable devices, and other healthcare data sources, healthcare organizations can use the results of predictive analytics to improve patient care, optimize resource allocation, and enhance overall healthcare delivery.

Predictive analysis is a data-driven approach that utilizes historical data and statistical algorithms to make informed predictions about future events. In the context of healthcare, predictive analysis involves extracting valuable patterns from huge amounts of patient data to anticipate patient outcomes, disease progression, and medical trends. Predictive analytics can identify individuals at high risk of having specific diseases based on their past medical records and history, genetics, lifestyle, and environmental factors. Early detection allows for proactive interventions, such as lifestyle changes, screenings, or preventive treatments, which can significantly reduce healthcare costs and improve patient outcomes. Healthcare providers can use this information to tailor treatment plans, allocate resources efficiently, and prioritize patient care. Predictive analytics can assess patient adherence to medication regimens by analyzing historical data and patient behavior.

The chapter explores the significance of predictive analysis in healthcare and its applications in Healthcare Policy and Planning. Policymakers can use predictive analysis to anticipate healthcare needs, allocate budgets, and plan for future healthcare infrastructure requirements. Predictive analysis is revolutionizing healthcare by enabling the forecasting of patient outcomes and medical trends. By harnessing the power of data and advanced analytics, healthcare providers, researchers, and policymakers can make more informed decisions, improve patient care, and contribute to the overall well-being of populations. As technology continues to advance and more data becomes available, the usage of predictive analysis in healthcare is expected to expand, offering even greater opportunities to enhance the quality and efficiency of healthcare delivery.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Healthcare, Machine learning, Predictive analysis.

INTRODUCTION

As technology advances daily, it continually permeates various aspects of our lives.

The field of health has witnessed significant developments over the years, with advancements spanning information gathering, treatments, and research. Information technology has provided medical professionals with innovative tools, introducing novel approaches to the practice of reshaping our behaviors in profound ways in medicine. Predictive Health Care combines the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of diseases through modern technology, which has undergone a transformative shift [1, 2].

Health Information Systems, with the combination of computer science, and healthcare, focus on optimizing the acquisition, storage, retrieval, and utilization of health data. This convergence has empowered physicians to enhance their ability to diagnose and treat patients, effectively. The continuous development in the evolution of technology in the health and medical sector has not only saved numerous lives but has also contributed to an ongoing improvement in the overall quality of life.

The advancement of technology has led to the improvement of both the quantity and quality of healthcare interventions. Efforts directed toward eradicating illnesses through precise diagnosis and effective treatment have resulted in significant progress.

Healthcare organizations worldwide face challenges such as cost reduction, improved coordination for efficient outcomes, accomplishing more with fewer resources, and adopting a more patient-centric approach [3]. Simultaneously, there is a growing realization that the healthcare industry contends with entrenched inefficiencies and suboptimal clinical outcomes. Developing competency in predictive analytics can empower these organizations to generate actionable insights, envision their future direction, enhance outcomes, and reduce the time required to achieve value.

Impact of Technology on Healthcare

The impact of technology on healthcare has been transformative, revolutionizing various aspects of the industry [4, 5]. Here are key areas where technology has made a significant impact:

Improved Patient Care

Electronic Health Records (EHR)

Digital records have replaced paper-based systems, enabling seamless and secure sharing of patient information among healthcare providers, resulting in more coordinated and efficient care.

Telemedicine

Technology facilitates remote consultations, enabling patients to access medical advice and treatment without the need for physical visits, particularly useful in rural or underserved areas.

Enhanced Diagnostics and Treatment

Medical Imaging

Advanced imaging technologies, such as MRI, CT scans, and ultrasound, provide detailed insights for accurate diagnostics and treatment planning.

Robot-Assisted Surgery

Robotics aid surgeons in performing minimally invasive procedures with precision, reducing recovery times and improving outcomes.

Medication Management

Digital Health Apps

Mobile applications help patients manage medications, track health metrics, and receive reminders, promoting adherence to treatment plans.

Telepharmacy

Remote pharmacy services enable patients to consult with pharmacists and receive medication guidance, improving access to pharmaceutical expertise.

Preventive Healthcare

Wearable Devices

Fitness trackers and health monitoring devices allow individuals to track their physical activity, monitor vital signs, and receive insights into their overall health.

Genomic Medicine

Advances in genomics enable personalized medicine, tailoring treatments based on an individual's genetic makeup for more effective and targeted interventions.

Big Data and Analytics

Predictive Analytics

Data analytics tools help predict disease outbreaks, identify high-risk populations, and optimize resource allocation for public health initiatives.

Population Health Management

Analyzing large datasets allows healthcare providers to identify trends, manage chronic diseases, and implement preventive measures for entire populations.

Improved Communication

Health Information Exchange (HIE)

Seamless sharing of patient information among healthcare providers ensures timely and coordinated care, reducing medical errors.

Secure Messaging

HIPAA-compliant communication platforms enable secure and efficient communication among healthcare professionals.

Enhanced Research and Development

Artificial Intelligence (AI)

AI and machine learning algorithms analyze large datasets, accelerating drug discovery, predicting patient outcomes, and aiding in medical research.

Virtual Trials

Technology facilitates remote participation in clinical trials, expanding the pool of participants and accelerating research timelines.

Patient Empowerment

Health Education Apps

Apps and online resources empower patients with information about their conditions, treatment options, and lifestyle choices.

Virtual Support Groups

Online communities provide emotional support and shared experiences for patients facing similar health challenges.

Efficiency and Cost Reduction

Healthcare Management Systems

Administrative tasks, billing, and scheduling are streamlined through digital systems, reducing paperwork and improving overall operational efficiency.

Remote Monitoring

Continuous monitoring of patients with chronic conditions at home helps prevent hospital readmissions, reducing healthcare costs.

Cyber Security Challenges

The increasing reliance on technology also brings challenges, including the need for robust cyber security measures to protect sensitive patient data from cyber threats.

Overall, the impact of technology on healthcare has been profound, enhancing patient outcomes, improving efficiency, and driving innovation across the entire healthcare ecosystem. The ongoing integration of technological advancements holds the promise of further transformative changes in the future.

Predictive Analysis and Healthcare

Predictive Analytics stands as the advanced analytics discipline employed to foresee outcomes of unknown future events. Drawing on methodologies from data mining, data modeling, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, it scrutinizes present data to make informed projections about what lies ahead. At the heart of predictive analytics is the predictor, a central variable gauging future behavior [6, 7]. Utilizing predictors, future probabilities are forecasted with a high degree of reliability, enhancing healthcare organizations; foresight into potential outcomes and aiding clinical decision-makers. In the medical realm, predictive analytics extends to forecasts on responses to medications and hospital readmission rates.

Predictive analytics plays a pivotal role in transforming and enhancing various aspects of healthcare. Here’s how predictive analytics aids the healthcare industry.

Disease Prevention and Early Intervention

Predictive analytics uses historical patient data, risk factors, and other variables to identify individuals at higher risk of developing specific diseases.

Healthcare providers can intervene early with preventive measures, screenings, and targeted interventions to reduce the impact of diseases.

Optimizing Treatment Plans

By analyzing patient data, predictive analytics helps in personalizing treatment plans based on individual characteristics and historical responses.

This ensures that healthcare providers can choose the most effective treatments, leading to better patient outcomes.

Reducing Hospital Readmissions

Predictive models can assess the similarities of the pattern of a patient being readmitted to the hospital after discharge. Healthcare providers can implement strategies to reduce readmissions by providing additional post-discharge support to high-risk patients.

Resource Allocation and Operational Efficiency

Predictive analytics assists in forecasting patient volumes, optimizing resource allocation, and improving overall operational efficiency. Hospitals can better plan staffing, manage bed utilization, and allocate resources effectively based on predicted future demands.

Chronic Disease Management

For patients with chronic conditions, predictive analytics helps in identifying those at higher risk of complications or exacerbations. This enables healthcare providers to tailor care plans, provide proactive interventions, and reduce the overall burden of chronic diseases.

Fraud Detection and Revenue Management

Predictive analytics is used to identify anomalies and patterns indicative of fraudulent activities in healthcare claims. This helps in reducing fraud, improving revenue cycle management, and ensuring financial integrity in healthcare organizations.

Personalized Medicine

Predictive analytics enables the development of personalized treatment plans based on an individual’s genetic makeup, lifestyle, and health history.

This approach maximizes treatment effectiveness and minimizes adverse reactions.

Population Health Management

Healthcare organizations use predictive analytics to identify trends and patterns within populations. This information aids in developing targeted public health initiatives, allocating resources efficiently, and addressing health disparities.

Enhancing Patient Engagement

Predictive analytics helps in understanding patient behavior, preferences, and engagement patterns. Healthcare providers can use this information to design personalized communication strategies, improving patient engagement and adherence to treatment plans.

Preparing for Public Health Challenges

Predictive analytics can forecast disease outbreaks, helping public health officials and healthcare providers prepare for and respond to public health crises effectively.

PRINCIPLES OF HEALTH PREDICTIVE ANALYSIS

Health forecasting is guided by four fundamental principles, each playing a crucial role in shaping the methodology and application of predictive models. These principles include:

Uncertainty and Error Measurement

Health forecasting inherently involves an element of uncertainty, recognizing that achieving a perfectly accurate prediction is virtually impossible. The measurement of uncertainty and error is a foundational principle, essential for validation and assessing the true value of a forecast. While data introduces uncertainties and errors, methodological approaches can mitigate these issues, ensuring health forecasts are as accurate as possible.

Focus of Health Forecasting

The focus of a health forecast pertains to the central issue under consideration. This principle emphasizes the importance of identifying the core health outcome being forecasted. For instance, health forecasts may target population health outcomes, such as life expectancy, or focus on individual cases, referred to as prognosis. The choice of focus is closely related to how data is aggregated in health forecasting.

Data Aggregation and Accuracy

The accuracy of health forecasting is influenced by how data is aggregated. Forecasting for population aggregates or groups poses fewer challenges than individual cases. By pooling the variances of population-related factors, even with individual variability, aggregated data tends to exhibit stable characteristics. Achieving higher accuracy in forecasting specific health events is thus more attainable when using aggregated population data compared to data specific to individuals.

Horizons of Health Forecasting

It refers to the period a forecast intended to cover, influenced by the demand for the forecast. Borrowing from other disciplines, health forecasting horizons are classified as short-term, medium-term, or long-term. These horizons are flexible and are often defined in relation to the qualitative indicator being forecast. For example, life expectancy forecasts or predictions of chronic disease prevalence may have long-range horizons, while routine health service uptake may involve short or medium-range horizons. Understanding and selecting the appropriate forecast horizon is crucial for effective healthcare service planning.

These principles not only have theoretical significance but also find practical applications in the literature. They guide the development of decision tools for health forecasting, considering factors such as the type, amount, and distribution of data required by predictive models, the forecast horizon, and the acceptable degree of accuracy or error. This approach provides a framework for developing health forecasting schemes with simple decision tools, facilitating informed and efficient decision-making in healthcare.

PATTERNS IN HEALTH PREDICTIVE ANALYSIS

Patterns of health data play a crucial role in forecasting and predicting health outcomes. The use of advanced analytics and machine learning techniques on health data has become increasingly prevalent, offering valuable insights for healthcare providers, researchers, and policymakers. Here are some key patterns of health data and their applications in forecasting:

Temporal Patterns

Applications

Predicting disease outbreaks, understanding seasonal variations, and identifying trends in patient data over time.

Example

Analyzing historical data to predict the peak seasons for influenza and allocate resources accordingly.

Spatial Patterns

Applications

Identifying geographical clusters of diseases, predicting disease spread across regions, and optimizing resource allocation.

Example

Using geographic information system (GIS) data to predict the spread of infectious diseases and plan vaccination campaigns.

Epidemiological Patterns

Applications

Forecasting the incidence and prevalence of diseases, understanding transmission dynamics, and implementing targeted interventions.

Example

Predicting the future prevalence of chronic diseases based on risk factors and demographic data.

Genetic Patterns

Applications

Predicting individual susceptibility to certain diseases, forecasting genetic predispositions, and guiding personalized medicine.

Example

Analyzing genetic data to predict the chances of developing diabetes or certain types of cancer, etc.

Social and Behavioral Patterns

Applications

Forecasting health behaviors, predicting adherence to treatment plans, and designing interventions to promote healthier lifestyles.

Example

Using social media data to analyze public sentiment and predict trends in mental health issues or outbreaks of certain diseases.

Clinical Patterns

Applications

Predicting patient outcomes, identifying early signs of deterioration, and optimizing treatment plans.

Example

Applying machine learning algorithms to electronic health records (EHR) data to predict patient readmissions or complications.

Environmental Patterns

Applications

Forecasting the impact of environmental factors on health, predicting the occurrence of environmental-related diseases.

Example

Analyzing air quality data to predict respiratory disease exacerbations.

Pharmacological Patterns

Applications

Forecasting drug interactions, predicting medication adherence, and optimizing drug discovery processes.

Example

Using pharmacogenomic data to predict individual responses to medications and personalize treatment plans.

Technological Patterns

Applications

Forecasting the impact of emerging technologies on healthcare, predicting the adoption of new medical interventions.

Example

Analyzing data on the usage of wearable devices to predict trends in remote patient monitoring.

Economic Patterns

Applications

Forecasting healthcare costs, predicting the economic impact of health interventions, and optimizing resource allocation.

Example

Using economic indicators to predict the financial burden of chronic diseases on healthcare systems.

By understanding and analyzing these patterns in health data, stakeholders in the healthcare ecosystem can make informed decisions, allocate resources effectively, and implement targeted interventions to improve health outcomes. Advanced analytics and machine learning algorithms are essential tools in leveraging these patterns for accurate forecasting and prediction in healthcare.

STEPS IN PREDICTIVE ANALYSIS MODELING

Predictive analytics modeling involves a systematic approach to developing models that can predict future outcomes based on historical data. Here are the key steps in predictive analytics modeling [8]:

Planning

Problem Definition

To define the problem statement clearly that the predictive model aims to address. Understand the business context and the specific goals of the prediction.

Data Collection

Collect relevant data needed to build the predictive model. This includes identifying the types of data (structured or unstructured) and sources.

Data Preparation

Data Cleaning

Cleanse the collected data to address issues like missing values, outliers, or inaccuracies. Ensuring data quality is crucial for the accuracy of the predictive model.

Feature Selection

Identify and select the most relevant features (variables) that contribute to the prediction. Feature engineering may involve transforming or creating new variables.

Model Building

Algorithm Selection

Select the appropriate predictive data modeling algorithm based on the nature of the problem, data characteristics, and the desired outcome. Common algorithms include linear regression, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks.

Training the Model

Use a portion of the prepared data (training dataset) to train the selected algorithm. The model learns patterns and relationships from historical data to make predictions.

Model Evaluation

Validation Dataset

Reserve a separate portion of the data (validation dataset) that the model has not seen during training. Evaluate the model's performance on this dataset to ensure it generalizes well to new, unseen data.

Metrics

Use appropriate evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, or area under the curve (AUC) depending on the nature of the prediction task.

Model Selection and Fine-Tuning

Hyperparameter Tuning

Adjust the hyperparameters of the model to optimize its performance. This may involve using techniques like grid search or randomized search to find the best hyperparameter values.

Comparing Models

If multiple algorithms were considered, we compare their performance on the validation dataset and choose the one that best meets the objectives.

Implementation

Deployment

Once the model’s performance is acceptable, deploy it in a real-world environment. This involves integration of the model into the existing systems where it can make predictions on input data.

Monitoring and Maintenance

Continuous Monitoring

Regularly monitor the predictive model's performance in a production environment. This includes tracking its predictions against actual outcomes and assessing whether the model is still relevant and accurate.

Model Maintenance

Update the model as needed, especially if there are changes in the data distribution, or business environment, or if new data becomes available.

Predictive Analytics Modeling

Predictive analytics modeling is an iterative process that may involve revisiting earlier steps based on insights gained during the model evaluation and deployment phases. The goal is to create a reliable and accurate model that can make informed predictions on future events or outcomes.

STEPS IN PREDICTIVE ANALYSIS MODELING IN HEALTHCARE

Step 1

Identify key concepts and ideas addressing a significant health condition with a substantial impact on healthcare services. Clearly define the health outcome to be predicted and specify the forecasting horizon, focusing on conditions that impose a considerable burden on the healthcare system.

Step 2

Leverage existing literature to pinpoint causal or highly correlated variables associated with the health outcome identified in Step 1. Expert consultation may be necessary to build domain knowledge and ensure a comprehensive understanding of relevant factors.

Step 3

Identify data sources for both the targeted health outcome (from Step 1) and potential predictor variables. Verify data availability and completeness, addressing any gaps in data series to ensure a robust dataset for analysis.

Step 4

Prepare datasets for basic statistical analyses and include the exploration of patterns and the development of forecast algorithms. Preliminary tasks involve data cleaning and management, along with the creation of secondary variables for further analysis.

Step 5

Generate predictive models and validate them using different sets of historical data with similar characteristics. Ensure the models are robust and capable of accurately forecasting the specified health outcome.

Step 6

Evaluate and finalize lists of indicators essential for effective predictive models based on practical access to their measures (data). Choose indicators that are feasible and reliable for incorporation into the forecasting process.

Step 7

Develop highly specific forecast services tailored to a particular purpose or client. Periodically update the models to ensure continued accuracy and relevance, accommodating shifts in data patterns and addressing changes in the health landscape.

Predictive Analysis in Healthcare Using Machine Learning

Machine learning algorithms demonstrate remarkable effectiveness in identifying intricate patterns within extensive datasets. Consequently, machine learning is frequently harnessed in diverse disease diagnosis and detection scenarios, contributing to more informed decisions about treatment plans and enhancing overall healthcare systems [9, 10]. Its crucial role spans across a myriad of radiology applications, streamlining the detection of intricate patterns and aiding radiologists in making well-informed decisions using data derived from conventional radiographs, CT scans, MRI images, PET scans, and radiology reports (Fig. 1).

Its pivotal role encompasses a wide array of radiology applications, streamlining the identification of intricate patterns and supporting radiologists in making informed decisions. It achieves this by analyzing data from conventional radiographs, CT scans, MRI images, PET scans, and radiology reports.

Fig. (1))
Steps in predictive analysis modeling in healthcare.

Predictions on Cardiovascular Diseases

Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) encompass a range of conditions affecting the heart or blood vessels. Given their significant global impact, predicting and diagnosing heart diseases is crucial. Machine learning techniques, including neural networks and genetic algorithms, have been instrumental in predicting heart diseases by leveraging major risk factors such as age, family history, diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol levels, smoking, alcohol intake, and obesity or physical inactivity. Various algorithms, including Naive Bayes, Neural Networks, and Decision Trees, have been applied to analyze medical datasets for heart disease prediction.

Diabetes Predictions

Diabetes mellitus, a chronic disease with widespread public health implications, has been a focus of machine learning predictions. Research efforts explore the relationship between lifestyle activities (eating habits, sleeping habits, physical activity) and diabetes risk [11]. Classification and Regression Trees (CART) machine learning algorithm, along with other classifiers such as Naïve Bayes and Support Vector Machines (SVM), have demonstrated effectiveness in diabetes dataset analysis, with SVM emerging as a robust classifier for medical datasets [12, 13].

Hepatitis Disease Prediction

Hepatitis, characterized by inflammation of liver cells, poses significant health risks. Machine learning methods, including a hybrid approach combining Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Simulated Annealing (SA), have been proposed for the diagnosis of hepatitis. Decision tree algorithms, such as C4.5, ID3, and CART, have been applied to categorize diseases and obtain accurate prediction results related to Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) protein cleavage sites.

Cancer Predictions Using Machine Learning

Cancer, a diverse group of diseases, has been the subject of extensive research for prognosis and prediction. Optimized models for breast cancer diagnosis and recurrence prediction have been developed using risk prediction algorithms. Machine learning techniques, including Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), have been applied to estimate survival rates and disease relapse for breast cancer patients. Comparative studies have identified SVM as a robust model for breast cancer recurrence prediction. Across various cancers, such as lung, skin, liver, and stomach cancers, data mining and machine learning techniques have been employed to predict prognosis and recurrence, emphasizing the importance of validating methods across multiple patient datasets [14-16].

In recent years, machine learning techniques have extended their applications to predicting diseases like asthma and tuberculosis (TB), and monitoring blood pressure, showcasing their versatility and potential for advancing healthcare predictions.

Predictive Analysis in Healthcare Using Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Predictive analysis in healthcare using artificial intelligence (AI) is a transformative approach that leverages advanced algorithms and machine learning models to forecast health-related outcomes, enhance decision-making, and optimize patient care. Here are key aspects and applications of predictive analysis in healthcare using AI:

Disease Diagnosis and Risk Prediction

Early Detection

AI algorithms can analyze patient data, including medical records, genetic information, and lifestyle factors, to identify patterns indicative of potential diseases at an early stage.

Risk Stratification

Predictive models help stratify patients based on their risk of developing specific conditions, allowing for targeted interventions and personalized preventive measures.

Patient Outcomes and Treatment Optimization

Outcome Prediction

AI models analyze patient data to predict potential outcomes of various treatments, aiding clinicians in selecting the most effective and personalized therapeutic strategies.

Treatment Recommendations

Predictive analysis assists in recommending optimal treatment plans by considering individual patient characteristics, treatment history, and response patterns.

Identifying At-Risk Patients

AI algorithms analyze historical patient data, to predict the likelihood of hospital readmission, which helps healthcare providers to intervene and implement preventive measures for at-risk individuals [17, 18].

Chronic Disease Management

Personalized Care Plans

AI-based predictive analysis helps create personalized care plans for patients with chronic conditions by considering their unique health profiles, adherence patterns, and response to interventions.

Remote Patient Monitoring

AI-driven predictive models enable continuous monitoring of patients with chronic diseases, allowing for early identification of potential complications and timely interventions.

Fraud Detection and Revenue Cycle Management

Anomaly Detection

AI algorithms analyze healthcare billing and claims data to detect anomalies and patterns indicative of fraudulent activities, optimizing revenue cycle management.

Enhanced Billing Accuracy

Predictive analysis helps identify potential billing errors and ensures accurate reimbursement for healthcare services.

Resource Allocation and Operational Efficiency

Demand Forecasting

AI models analyze historical data to predict patient admission rates, enabling hospitals to optimize resource allocation, staffing, and bed management.

Supply Chain Optimization

Predictive analysis assists in forecasting the demand for medical supplies, optimizing inventory levels, and ensuring efficient supply chain management.

Drug Discovery and Development

Identifying Targets

AI-driven predictive models analyze biological data to identify potential drug targets that accelerates the drug discovery process.

Clinical Trial Optimization

Predictive analysis assists in patient selection for clinical trials, optimizing trial design, and increasing the likelihood of successful drug development.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) for Unstructured Data

Extracting Insights from Text

NLP algorithms analyze unstructured data from clinical notes, research articles, and patient narratives to extract valuable insights, supporting predictive analysis.

Sentiment Analysis

NLP techniques assess patient sentiment and feedback, providing additional context for predictive models in healthcare decision-making [19].

The integration of AI and predictive analysis in healthcare not only enhances clinical decision support but also contributes to more efficient healthcare operations, personalized patient care, and advancements in medical research and drug development. As technology continues to evolve, the potential for AI-driven predictive analysis to revolutionize healthcare outcomes remains promising.

CHALLENGES IN PREDICTIVE ANALYSIS IN HEALTHCARE

The importance of health forecasting has been recognized in previous discussions, but various challenging issues must be addressed in its development and application. These challenges include limitations in the breadth and reliability of health data, the resilience of health forecasting tools and techniques, and a noticeable lack of demand for health forecasting.

Despite recent technological advancements that make measuring health indicators more affordable and convenient, the efficient capture and accessibility of crucial population health indicators remain inadequate and invalidated. In personalized medicine, prognostic effects are influenced by numerous complex factors, some of which are unknown, and these factors often intertwine randomly, presenting a challenge in developing a reliable health forecast.

In addition to data and methodological limitations, convincingly demonstrating the performance of a health forecasting model in realistic settings is challenging. While health forecasting research has focused on methods for forecasting aggregate health conditions or specific situations, such as crowding in emergency departments and total admissions, the optimal value lies in condition-specific health forecasts.

Tailoring forecasts to particular health conditions allows healthcare providers to make more informed decisions and preparations. For instance, the United Kingdom Meteorological Office provides a specific health forecast service to some Primary Care Trusts (PCT) for conditions like COPD, showcasing the value of such specialized services, even though they are currently rare.

The effectiveness of health forecasts is the most evident when they offer ample warning for timely remedial action. Healthcare providers make critical decisions and allocate resources based on the potential demand for healthcare services, ranging from basic social care for early symptoms to using advanced staff and facilities for extreme events. Meeting the demand for a health forecast that allows sufficient time for preparatory activities necessitates the use of a reliable forecasting technique and ample data. However, this comes with the challenge of balancing precision and accuracy in the forecast. Thus, finding a delicate balance between predictability and the demand for specific health forecasts is a key challenge in health forecasting.

Another challenge relates to the practical use of health forecasts. These forecasts are developed to cater to the needs of vulnerable individuals or institutions (health care providers). An intelligent early warning system that can effectively communicate forecasts to users is essential. Some health forecast services have been delivered through automated telephone services, home visits/treatment, and direct communication of forecasts to individuals and service providers.

CONCLUSION

Health forecasting is a dynamic and continuously evolving process that requires frequent updates, incorporating innovative techniques and data while adhering to established principles. Current methodologies primarily involve time series analyses using smoothing or moving average models. Additionally, less probabilistic forecasting models like Quantile Regression Mapping (QRM) offer a viable alternative for predicting and anticipating extreme health events. Despite the significance of the horizons of health forecasting, their classification in the literature is lacking, resulting in an absence of common benchmarks to guide new health forecasts.

The utilization of patterns within health data through techniques such as time series analysis or other probabilistic methods proves instrumental in health forecasting. However, despite being a valuable resource for enhancing and promoting health service provision, health forecasting is not without its drawbacks. Challenges may arise from issues related to data sources, methodologies, or technology. This overview aims to stimulate further discussions on standardizing health forecasting approaches and methods, with the goal of establishing it as a robust tool that facilitates healthcare and health services delivery with greater effectiveness and uniformity

Prediction and Analysis of Digital Health Records, Geonomics, and Radiology Using Machine Learning



Sundeep Raj1, *, Arun Prakash Agarwal1, Sandesh Tripathi2, Nidhi Gupta1
1 Sharda School of Engineering & Technology, Sharda University, Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh-201306, India
2 Birla Institute of Applied Sciences, Bhimtal, Nainital, Uttarakhand-263136, India

Abstract

Building different machine learning algorithms and their potential applications to enhance healthcare systems is very important. AI has countless uses in healthcare, including the analysis of medical data, early disease diagnosis and detection, evidence-based objectives to minimize human error, reducing errors between and among observers, risk identification and interventions for healthcare management, health monitoring in real-time, helping patients and clinicians choose the right medication, and assessing drug responses. Machine learning techniques have transformed many facets of healthcare, ranging from new tools that allow people to better control their health to new models that assist physicians in making more accurate decisions. Since the advent of the pacemaker and the first computerized records for blood test results and chest X-ray reports by Kaiser in the 1950s, physicians have seen the potential of algorithms to save lives. As new developments in image processing, deep learning, and natural language processing are revolutionizing the healthcare sector, this rich history of machine learning for healthcare feeds innovative research today.

It is necessary to comprehend the human effects of machine learning, including transparency, justice, regulation, simplicity of deployment, and integration into clinical processes, in order to use it to enhance patient outcomes. The application of machine learning for risk assessment and diagnosis, illness progression modeling, enhancing clinical workflows, and precision medicine will be covered in this chapter, which starts with an introduction to clinical care and data. We shall include all methodological details for each of these covering topics like algorithmic fairness, causal inference, off-policy reinforcement learning, interpretability of ML models, and the foundations of deep learning on imaging and natural language.

Advances in AI and ML technologies have significantly improved the ability to forecast and recognize health emergencies, disease conditions, disease populations, and immunological responses, to name a few. Even though there is still doubt about the usefulness of ML-based techniques and how to interpret their findings in clinical contexts, their use is spreading quickly. Here, we provide a succinct introduction to machine learning-based methodologies and learning algorithms, such as reinforcement learning, supervised learning, and unsupervised learning, with examples. Subsequently, we explore the applications of machine learning (ML) in various healthcare domains such as genetics, neuroimaging, radiology, and electronic health records. Along with offering ideas for potential future uses, we also skim the surface regarding the dangers and difficulties associated with applying machine learning to the healthcare industry, including issues of privacy and ethics.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Genomics, HER, Healthcare, Machine learning, Support vector machine.

INTRODUCTION

During the 1950s, the first Artificial intelligence machine was proposed by Alan Turing [1], which marked the beginning of machine learning applications. Machine learning was first used for face detection for security services [2], and it has since been utilised in public transit to increase efficiency and lower danger [3, 4] as well as more recently in a variety of biotechnology and healthcare applications [5]. Similar developments are predicted for medicine and healthcare. Machine learning and artificial intelligence have substantially altered daily life and corporate processes. This field has made remarkable strides recently, offering doctors relief from workloads and increasing precision, prognosis, and care quality.

The potential of a doctor or an analyst is to perform their own duties, recognize trends in healthcare, and create models for disease prediction which are mostly aided by recent advances in machine learning. Machine learning-based techniques have additionally been put into practice in large medical organizations in order to attain higher efficiency in the following areas: blood samples [5], identification of irregularities in organs [6-8], robot-assisted surgeries [9, 10], and bones [11], as well as the organization of health records electronically. Recently in the fight against COVID-19, hospital response times have been accelerated by the use of machine learning algorithms.

With GE's Clinical Command Centre, a deep learning technology, hospitals were capable of exchanging, tracking, and organizing patients, rooms, beds, EHRs, ventilators, as well as staff throughout the pandemonium [12]. Artificial intelligence has also been utilized by researchers to monitor and identify SARS-CoV2 genetic sequences and to create vaccinations [13].

As the medical sector expands into the modern technological era, numerous innovations appear. Advancements in the discipline, such as faster diagnostic times, greater accuracy, and ease of use, depend heavily on machine learning and artificial intelligence models and applications. Outlining the drawbacks and benefits of methods based on machine learning in the healthcare sector is the aim of this chapter.

We hope to give a concise summary of the many machine learning approaches and draw attention to the regions where these types of methods are mainly used since the healthcare business is engulfed in the use of new machine learning technologies. We talk about their extensive potential and application for the development of the future of the healthcare sector. We discuss the risks and challenges that arise from their application in terms of ethics and logistics.

OVERVIEW OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

While artificial intelligence, deep learning, and machine learning are sometimes used synonymously, they refer to distinct sets of algorithms and learning processes. The general name for any computerised intelligence that mimics and learns from human intelligence is Artificial Intelligence (AI) [14]. While self-driving cars and robots are the most well-known examples of autonomous technology, AI is also used in many commonplace applications, including web searches and personalised marketing. Due to Artificial Intelligence's increased levels of decision-making, precision, problem-solving capacity, and computing skills, AI application and development have made great leaps in recent years and have been applied to many domains [15].

In the process of developing Artificial Intelligence algorithms, the collected data is divided into two sets—a training set and a test set—in order to guarantee impartial forecasts, populations representative, and trustworthy learning. The training set, as its name implies, is used to train algorithms. It consists of sets of defining characteristics (data points) and, in the type of supervised learning, correlating predictions. The testing data set, which is basically new to the algorithm, is only used to evaluate its performance. This step is used to ensure that biases in the training dataset's algorithm testing are eliminated [16]. When an algorithm produces satisfactory results during training and testing, it is put into use in healthcare environments.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread and has numerous applications in various sub-regions; here, we give a summary of two of these sub-regions: deep learning and machine learning.

Machine learning is the application of various algorithms and statistical methods to address issues without the necessity for specialised programming [17]. Since many machine learning models have only one layer, a significant part of data processing feature extraction must be finished before the data is entered into the algorithm [18]. These types of machine learning techniques, in the absence of the additional layers, necessitate extensive data preparation to identify accurate predictions and prevent the training dataset from being over- or under-fitted.

Deep learning is treated as a more complex subset of machine learning in which users make use of layered artificial neural networks. It offers more precision and interpretability at the expense of less interpretability [19]. According to its description, the neural network approach uses a multilayer network to support the connections between the units or artificial neurons, in each of the layers and the layers above and below [20]. These multilevel links let these networks analyse data autonomously, allowing them to learn, perceive, and draw conclusions from it. The data are processed until specific outcomes are obtained.

Different Learning Methodologies

The majority of AI and machine learning algorithms are based on several learning methodologies. Supervised learning is one subtype that is used to train algorithms for prediction and classification using prior instances or outputs. The fact that the training set for this learning method includes features and matching predictions, or outcomes, is a key differentiator. In short, supervised learning method uses details derived from the features of training data set to building an outcome-predicting model accurately from the training data set. The learned model is then used to utilize the new testing data set attributes to create predictions.

Some machine learning algorithms that use supervised learning approaches are Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and Artificial Neural Networks. Using a single node as the starting point, decision tree algorithms create a decision assistance tool that shows the potential outcomes of it. After making that decision and subsequent ones, the tree continues until it reaches the desired outcome [21]. Classification techniques called Support Vector Machines (SVM) identify the biggest margin hyperplane for dividing data and provide the best fit for arranging it. SVMs employ supervised learning for classifying features in two group issues [22]. Three layers make up artificial neural networks, or ANNs: input, output, and one or more hidden layers. Each layer's neurons are linked to every other layer's neurons both ahead and behind it [23]. Supervised machine learning techniques are extensively used in the healthcare industry for a variety of purposes, including image detection, hospital outcome identification, and disease prediction.

Unsupervised learning, which is commonly employed for data evaluation and application clustering, is another subset of AI-based learning techniques. When it comes to data analysis, stratification, and reduction, unsupervised machine learning is typically used for goals other than prediction. In general, algorithms are used in unsupervised clustering techniques to organize data into separate groups that have not yet been identified. Despite the fact that most machine learning approaches involve feature extraction and preprocessing of the data before the input, this approach enables feature extraction and investigates potential data clusters by finding the underlying features or relationships of the data and then classifying them according to their similarities.

Deep Belief Networks (DBN), CNN (Convolutional neural networks), and the k-means method are a few unsupervised learning techniques. k-Means algorithm is the most popular unsupervised learning algorithm, which is employed as a clustering technique to find the mean across groups in unlabeled type of datasets and form groups according to the mean. Deep belief network (DBN) is a multilayer network with several hidden layers that are responsible for the feature recognition and correlation analysis in the data. It is composed of intra-level connections that are helpful for the data retrieval and is usually based on unsupervised learning [24, 25]. Since convolutional neural networks (CNNs) rely on feature recognition and identification, they are multilayer networks that function well for image recognition, anomaly detection, and identification.

Because the data is homogeneous and there are no predetermined results, several unsupervised algorithms are utilised for clustering; nonetheless, despite their usefulness and speed, unsupervised techniques are only marginally popular in the healthcare industry.

Another technique for learning that falls between supervised and unsupervised learning is reinforcement learning. This learning is reliant on reward sequences, much like the psychological mechanisms of conditioning, and it develops a strategy for functioning within a particular problem domain. Reinforcement learning approaches have been called the closest to animal and human learning since they optimise the error criteria and have the ability to affect their surroundings [26].

The choice of learning methods is typically determined by the implementation goal and is comparatively less complex than the choice of algorithms given the variety of learning approaches. The Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is a popular neural network that makes use of reinforcement learning. An RNN is a type of neural network in which all artificial neurons are connected to one another. This allows the artificial neurons to reuse the outputs of one phase as input for another and to receive inputs with time delays. Translation, time series prediction, rhythm acquisition, speech recognition, as well as creation of music are among its many applications.

Even while the use of reinforcement learning in healthcare is still restricted because of its requirements for structure, diverse data, the formulation and application of the rewards, and large computational resources, still it has the potential to significantly advance in the field.

A viable solution that is relevant to the healthcare application must be identified and implemented, given the variety of deep learning and machine learning approaches available. The amount of sample size [27, 28], features, and data distributions [29] are a few variables that need to be taken into account as they have a significant effect on the processes of learning and forecasting.

Healthcare Applications of Artificial Intelligence

The sector of healthcare has been seeing advances in machine learning for years. AI applications have the potential to help with a variety of tasks, including case triage as well as diagnosis [30], improved image segmentation and scanning [31], decision-making support, neuroimaging, and illness risk prediction. Here, we provide a quick rundown of the latest developments in Artificial Intelligence applications to particular areas of health care. The greater availability of the digital data utilised in ML-based techniques and the apps' clinical applications and experiments in addition to learning methodologies serve as the basis for inclusion criteria for the applications listed.

In the current study, we concentrated on the application of Machine Learning in the domains of medical imaging, genetic engineering, and electronic healthcare records. These domains also embody the BIG data in healthcare, namely the organised and disorganised data within the field, and have demonstrated noteworthy potential concerning clinical implementations.

The following is the search approach we will use: articles published between the months of June 2020 and December 2020; journal databases and online libraries, such as Academic, OneFile, Nature, Gale, Science Direct, Pubmed, and PsycNet. The papers and articles in the compilation concentrated on the present and future applications of Artificial Intelligence and machine learning for the healthcare industry. The search terms that came up were artificial intelligence for healthcare, medical imaging with machine learning, machine learning and big data, electronic health records, genomics with machine learning, medical applications of AI, and problems with AI in healthcare.

Digital Health Records

In the 1960s, Lockheed introduced the first electronic health record (EHR), which was first called a clinical information system [32]. The systems had undergone numerous reconstructions since then in an effort to establish a uniform system for the industry. To increase the quality and productivity of the work, the US federal government invested billions of dollars in 2009 to encourage the implementation of EHRs in all practices. As a result, by 2015, nationwide almost 87 percent office-based applications had integrated EHRs into their systems [33]. Deep learning applications, such as prescription refills and the use of patient history to forecast diagnoses, have benefited greatly from BIG data gathered by EHR systems with feature data that is structured.

Physician diagnosis and treatment have been aided by this, which has led to notable advancements in the organization of data, accessibility of data, and quality. Researchers’ access to health records has been facilitated by the standardisation of features across databases.

Scientists created models using deep learning for diagnosis as well as prediction of clinical disorders using EHRs because they recognize the critical role played in therapy delivery using prediction. In a recent research, Zhang, Liu, and Razavian created an algorithm using deep learning to predict the occurrence of diseases like a failure of heart, stroke, and renal failure, utilizing CNNs (supervised learning) and LSTM networks (reinforcement learning).

This method employed both structured data by the EHR and unstructured data by the progress and diagnostic notes, in contrast to prior prediction models. Liu et al. (40,00) expounded that adding unstructured data into the model led to noteworthy enhancements in all the baseline accuracy metrics, hence underscoring the resilience and adaptability of these types of algorithms. Ge and his colleagues developed a model for predicting post-stroke pneumonia between 7 to 14 days in another study that used deep neural network approaches.

With an accuracy of 92.8 percent for 7th day prediction and 90.5 percent for 14th day predictions, the model yielded a highly accurate model for forecasting pneumonia after a stroke happened (AUC, model performance measure by combining the specificity and sensitivity of a model) [34]. In order to forecast mortality in intensive care unit patients, a number of machine learning (ML) models have also been used. Ahmad and associates have demonstrated a high degree of predictive capacity in one of these models for predicting death rates among patients with paralytic ileus (PI, an incomplete intestinal blockage that impedes food transit and ultimately results in a buildup and total intestinal blockage) using electronic health records.

When predicting mortality for patients with peripheral artery disease, the algorithm known as the SRML - Statistically Robust Machine Learning based Predictor for Mortality has an accuracy rate of 81.30% [35]. By utilising EHR prediction algorithms, healthcare providers and patients can make more informed decisions about clinical treatment when they are armed with expected mortality.

Radiology

Medical imaging or radiology has made remarkable progress using machine learning techniques to several imaging modalities, which include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), X-ray, ultrasound, and many more. This is due to the fact that data is digital and that structured data formats are available as DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine). To identify lesions [36], tumors [37, 38], fractures [39, 40] and rips [41, 42], several machine learning models have been constructed.

McKinney and associates have employed an algorithm using deep learning in a new study to identify tumours at an earlier stage of growth based on mammograms. These deep learning-based screen techniques enable a higher rate of tumour resection by identifying and localising tumours at an earlier stage of breast cancer than would be possible with traditional screening methods. An AUC score of 11.5% allowed the method based on deep learning to beat seasoned radiologists with direct comparison [43]. With differing degrees of effectiveness, a number of additional studies have also used Machine Learning techniques for the identification of breast cancer. These studies include models by Ahmad and others [44], Wang and others [45], and Amrane and others [46].

Similar to this, Esteva and associates employed CNN (unsupervised learning) in recent work to categorize 2032 distinct skin conditions using dermoscopic pictures. The accuracy of the data was further supported by an impartial comparison by CNN's categorization with dermatologists certified by 21 board, which revealed performance “on par”. This method can lead to early diagnosis and ease of use when combined with the typical consumer mobile platform. Simultaneously, research has employed machine learning (ML) techniques to measure the advancement of retinal disorders [46-48]. Arcadu et al. conducted a study wherein they utilised a CNN using deep learning to identify the aneurysms responsible for visual loss resulting from the advancement of DR (Diabetic Retinopathy) [49]. Despite not being specifically designed to do so, the CNN was also capable of identifying tiny, low-contraction microaneurysms [49, 50]. Diabetic retinopathy called a prevalent eye disorder affects 60% of people with type-1 diabetes [51]. Consequently, it can be challenging to identify in its early stages. Timely prediction made possible by the CNN technique may help patients avoid or postpone permanent visual loss. For decades, X-rays have been used to detect lung diseases and anomalies in the chest cavity; however, a thorough, meticulous examination by a qualified radiologist is frequently necessary. In an effort to replicate the detection made by skilled radiologists, Rajpurkar and colleagues recently carried out a retrospective description for investigating the abilities of a convolutional neural network with 121-layer to analyse a set of chest x-rays with kinds of thoracic diseases and for identifying abnormalities.

Comparatively, CNN performed 2% better than radiologists in terms of identification accuracy of 81%. This study, like CNNs developed by Asif and others [52], Tsai and Tao [53], Lee and colleagues [54], and Liang and colleagues [55], shows the tremendous support that these methods may provide in diagnosing and examining illnesses, further reduced the burden on healthcare professionals, even though they are applied retrospectively.

In addition, ML-based methods have been used to diagnose and predict the course of serious mental illnesses such as depression [56], psychosis [57, 58], PTSD [59], Parkinson's disease [60, 61], Alzheimer's disease [62], and various developmental disorders such as ADHD [63, 64] and autism [65, 66].

In one of the works, utilising structural MRI scans, Faturrahman, and others proposed a higher-level model by using DBNs (unsupervised learning) for predicting the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with 90.59% sensitivity, 91.76% accuracy, and 92.96% specificity [67]. While there is not a treatment for AD, early detection can aid in the implementation of plans to halt the deterioration and symptoms. Patel and others created a model for predicting depression diagnosis as well as treatment response by using the decision tree method and feature-rich type of data sets including cognitive behaviour scores, functional MRI, and age. For diagnostic and treatment responses, the model received scores of 87.27% and 89.47%, respectively [68]. By using this predictive diagnosis, depression patients can be identified, and tailored treatment regimens can be created based on their individual reactions. Because of its clear benefits in classification, accuracy, specificity and sensitivity, in diagnosis and prediction, machine learning (ML) has a lot of scope for it in the medical profession. This is demonstrated by the current uses of ML in medical imaging.

Genetic Engineering and Genomics

Genetic engineering has flourished since the innovation of the adaptable DNA system, which is known as Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) [69]. This discovery of “programmable endonucleases” has greatly reduced the cost of genetic engineering, streamlined the process of genetic alteration, and aided in the process of diagnosis [70]. Although the tool is not flawless, the current use of CRISPR to Cas (CRISPR-associated protein) editing, such as Cas-13a, and Cas-9 [71] has altered genetic editing. Recently, a number of machine learning methods for anticipating off-target changes in Cas9 gene editing have been developed.

By utilising deep FFs (AUC score: 97%), and deep CNNs (AUC score: 97.2%) a new program created by Ka-Chun Wong and Jiecong Lin has enhanced the accuracy of predictions made by machine learning [72]. Scientists are utilising Cas9 to create activity predictors and more dependable Cas9 variants in an effort to decrease error, given the potential for error and off-target alterations while utilising this technology. These models include RNA design tools guided by deep learning [73-77], hyper-accurate Cas9 variants [78], and Cas9 variants with improved accuracy and fidelity [79-81].

In addition to CRISPR gene editing, O'Brien and associates have created a service that offers efficiency in nucleotide editing by utilising supervised learning and random forest algorithms to examine how various nucleotide compositions affect the effectiveness of homology-directed repair, or HDR [82].

To determine the most effective way to precisely identify where to insert a certain point mutation and forecast HDR efficiency, they created the Computational Universal Nucleotide Editor (CUNE). Moreover, Pan and associates have created the ToxDL gene editing prediction model, which employs a CNN methodology to forecast protein toxicity in vivo based solely on sequence data [83]. Pharacogenomics, a different area of genetic engineering, has also made great progress in using Artificial Intelligence and ML to establish stable dosages of increasingly popular drugs [84-86].

In one such trial, to lower the risk of acute rejection in patients receiving kidney transplants, Tang and others used an ML-based technique to find a stable Tacrolimus dose [87]. Recently, oncology [88], psychiatry [89], neurology [90], and bariatrics [91], have all used machine learning in pharmacogenomics.

The fight against COVID-19 has also benefited greatly from genetic engineering applications of machine learning. Malone et al. conducted a recent study wherein they employed machine learning algorithms-based software to foretell which anti-genes possess the necessary characteristics of HLA-binding, processing, cell surface presentation, and T-cell recognition potential to be suitable for clinical aims for immunotherapy.

The group was able to effectively characterize both the “entire SARS-CoV2 proteome” and epitope hotspots by utilizing immunogenicity predictions from this technique in conjunction with antigen delivery to the infected host tissue. These findings provide guidelines for creating vaccinations against the virus that are universally applicable to all members of the world's population.

CHALLENGES AND RISKS

Applications of machine learning in healthcare present innovative and progressive opportunities, but additionally, they raise unusual risks, challenges, and a healthy cynicism. We go over the primary risk factors here, including the possibility of prediction error and its effects, system security, and privacy vulnerabilities, despite the deficiency of information to generate consistent results. Among the difficulties are moral dilemmas, the removal of the human element from healthcare, as well as the interpretability and usefulness of the methods in a bedside environment.

The dependence of machine learning algorithms on probabilistic distributions and the likelihood of inaccuracy in diagnosis and prediction represent a significant danger.

A reasonable amount of uncertainty regarding the accuracy and validity of predictions given by ML-based approaches is also sparked by this. The consequences of using machine learning (ML) techniques that lead to a human’s death are dire, notwithstanding the fact that mistakes and probability likelihood are inherent in many facets of health care. A possible resolution would be to require stringent institutional and legal clearance from several organisations prior to implementing these machine learning-based techniques [92, 93]. Another strategy that can be used to prevent false-negative or false-positive diagnoses in extremely sensitive applications is human intervention and supervision by a qualified healthcare professional (e.g., diagnosis of breast cancer or depression).

When current healthcare professionals are involved in the development and application of these strategies, adaptation rates may rise, and worries about declining career possibilities or a diminishing workforce may subside [94].

A potential concern when utilising machine learning and deep learning techniques for the medical field is the lack of sufficient training and testing datasets with sufficiently big sample numbers to guarantee good prediction reproducibility and reliability. It is critical to emphasize the relevance of high-quality data because machine learning and deep learning algorithms 'learn' from the data. Furthermore, many learning networks and techniques require vast amounts of feature-rich data, which are not easily accessible and might potentially represent a limited sample of the population.

Furthermore, the data obtained from a variety of healthcare domains are diverse, lacking, and have a much higher number of features than samples. While creating and analysing the outcomes of techniques based on ML-based, these difficulties must be carefully considered. These obstacles might be addressed with the help of open science and the current movement for research data sharing. The risk to privacy and moral ramifications of using Healthcare applications of ML-based techniques should also be considered. Many machine learning (ML) techniques are developed and implemented using cloud-based platforms, with the understanding that these methods necessitate a significant amount of computing power as well as large-scale, readily scalable data storage.

Prior to developing any models, one of the first things that should be taken into consideration is enhanced data security and accountability, in light of privacy concerns and the delicate nature of medical data.

Regarding ethical considerations, scientists utilising machine learning techniques in the healthcare industry can easily draw insights from the genetic engineering domain, which has experienced a great deal of ethical discussion. There is an ongoing debate concerning the viability of using genetic engineering for genetic improvements which are long-lasting. Finding and correcting deleterious genetic abnormalities, like the HTT variant, which causes Huntington's disease, may be able to treat disorders like these with potentially fatal outcomes [95].

On the other hand, developing therapies that modify a person's genome and the genome of their progeny while they are still prohibitively expensive could exacerbate the socioeconomic divide for those who cannot afford such care [96]. Guidelines for the creation of AI machines have just recently surfaced. An Artificial Intelligence Model Governance Framework was developed by Singapore in 2019 to help private sector companies develop and apply AI in an ethical way [97]. Additionally, an executive order was issued by the US government to “maintain American leadership in artificial intelligence” and to regulate the development of AI [98]. These rules and principles, notwithstanding their severity, are in place to guarantee the conduct and advancement of ethical research.

Interpreting the results and determining if they are clinically applicable presents a significant challenge when applying machine learning to healthcare. Because machine learning (ML)-based approaches, especially deep learning-based approaches, have complex structures, it becomes very challenging to separate and identify the original features' contribution towards the prediction. The flexibility of ML-based techniques in healthcare has been severely hampered by a lack of transparency, despite the fact that it might not cause too much concern for other ML applications (like web searches). In the healthcare industry, the strategy for a solution is equally important as the real solution.

Increased adoption rates may also result from the participation of medical professionals and doctors in the creation, use, and testing of machine learning-based techniques. Furthermore, while there exists a reasonable degree of doubt regarding the possibility of a weakened interpersonal bond between a patient and primary care physician because of the growing adoption of machine learning-based techniques, these approaches offer a singular chance to enhance involvement. Research indicates that the notion of the physician-patient connection is gradually diminishing, with almost 25% of Americans lacking a primary care physician [99]. Here, machine learning (ML) can offer special chances to boost patient participation in discussions about potential diagnoses and improve the effectiveness of Outreach Programmes.

When individuals speak with their PCPs, they could discover that early diagnosis provided by ML-based techniques also aids in the development of a healthy way of life. Lastly, according to a poll aimed at physicians, 5 percent of them spent fewer than nine minutes with their patients, and 56% of them spent 16 minutes or less [100]. Reduced anxiety and more time spent one-on-one with patients are two benefits of using AI approaches for diagnosis and symptom monitoring. These improvements will enhance patient satisfaction and results.

CONCLUSION

Even though the summary highlights the progress made in machine learning, much more work needs to be done in this area. The goal of many recent machine learning advancements in the medical field is to assist doctors and other healthcare professionals in providing patients with better care that is delivered more quickly, accurately, and with greater quality. To overcome the unavailability of data, the issues associated with constructing machine learning algorithms may be addressed by either designing and making improvements in data collection, dissemination, and storage or by algorithm development for handling unstructured data. Future developments may result in more accessible healthcare for lower-class countries and populations, as well as more economical medical exams and imaging systems. These developments could put an end to health inequities.

Improvements in the identification and dose of medications, the prediction of individual drug responses, and the application of genetic engineering to treat hereditary illnesses and mutations are all anticipated by scientists. ML has the potential to rethink patient care and strengthen the role of doctors. The present ML algorithms can serve as an excellent basis for ML's future advancements and use in the medical field, under the condition that the risks and challenges associated with its future use are acknowledged and addressed.
