The type and qualities of the data as well as the functionality of the learning algorithms determine how effective and efficient a machine learning solution is. To efficiently construct data-driven systems, machine learning algorithms can be used in the areas of classification analysis, regression, data clustering, feature engineering and dimensionality reduction, association rule learning, or reinforcement learning. It is therefore difficult to choose an appropriate learning algorithm that fits the intended application in each domain. The explanation for this is that various learning algorithms have distinct goals, and even within the same category, the results of various learning algorithms can differ based on the properties of the data [7].

To apply machine learning algorithms in a variety of real-world application areas, including cybersecurity services, IoT systems, smart cities, healthcare and COVID-19, context-aware systems, sustainable agriculture, and many more, it is crucial to understand the underlying principles of these algorithms.

An illustration of the application of Machine Learning in healthcare is explained below:

Application of Machine Learning in Healthcare

In several medical fields, including disease prediction, medical information extraction, finding patterns in data, patient management, etc., machine learning can assist in resolving diagnostic and prognostic issues [8, 9]. WHO [9] states that coronavirus illness (COVID-19) is an infectious condition brought on by a recently identified coronavirus. In the fight against COVID-19, learning strategies have gained popularity recently [10, 11]. Learning techniques are applied to the COVID-19 pandemic to categorize high-risk patients, their mortality rate, and other abnormalities. In addition, it can be applied to disease diagnosis and treatment, COVID-19 outbreak forecasting, and a deeper understanding of the virus's origin [12, 13]. Researchers can predict where and when COVID-19 will spread with the use of machine learning, and they may alert those areas to make the necessary preparations.

ROLE OF MACHINE LEARNING IN HEALTHCARE

Within the healthcare sector, the significance of machine learning algorithms lies in their ability to interpret the immense volumes of healthcare data generated daily through electronic health records. Integrating machine learning into healthcare practices allows us to unveil intricate patterns and glean insights from medical data that would be exceptionally challenging to discern manually. As the integration of machine learning in healthcare proliferates, healthcare providers can transition toward a more predictive approach to precision medicine. This evolution leads to a more cohesive system that not only elevates care delivery but also enhances patient outcomes and streamlines patient-oriented processes.

Among healthcare professionals, the most prevalent applications utilizing machine learning include medical billing automation, providing clinical decision support, and formulating guidelines for clinical practice. For instance, at MD Anderson Cancer Center, data scientists have introduced an innovative solution that employs deep learning to determine acute toxicities in patients experiencing radiation therapy for head and neck cancers. In clinical workflows, the integration of deep learning in healthcare facilitates the automatic recognition of intricate patterns in medical data, furnishing primary care providers with clinical decision support directly within the electronic health record [14].

Automating and Streamlining Processes

In the realm of healthcare, machine learning holds the potential to automate and optimize various procedures. In practical terms, ML can handle vast amounts of medical data, automatically generating customized treatment plans for patients. This not only saves time and effort but also enhances the quality of patient care. Furthermore, the technology proves valuable in tasks such as monitoring medical resources and optimizing staff schedules, contributing to overall improvements in efficiency and patient well-being.

Tailoring Treatment Approaches

Machine learning analyzes individual medical histories, symptoms, and test results, enabling healthcare providers to deliver personalized treatment to patients. Medical professionals can leverage ML to formulate tailored treatment plans and prescribe medications targeting specific ailments in individuals. This technology also grants healthcare companies access to insightful analyses based on electronic health information, empowering clinicians to make more informed and precise decisions regarding suitable treatments for patients.

Cost Reduction

By automating routine tasks and improving accuracy, machine learning helps healthcare organizations cut costs associated with manual labor and medical errors. Additionally, ML helps to identify patients who could be prone to chronic conditions, facilitating early intervention and preventive care, thereby reducing long-term healthcare expenses.

Tracing Payments Fraud

Approximately 3% of healthcare claims in the US are false, resulting in an annual loss of $100 billion, according to the Justice Department. Machine learning plays a crucial role in expediting the approval, processing, and payment of valid claims by identifying false ones before reimbursement. ML not only safeguards patient data but also detects and prevents insurance fraud, as exemplified by leading institutions like Harvard Pilgrim Health, utilizing ML-based fraud detection systems.

Enhancing Patient Satisfaction

Through personalized treatment, reduced waiting times, and minimized medical errors, machine learning contributes to an enhanced patient experience in healthcare organizations. The result is improved patient satisfaction and outcomes.

Early Disease Detection

Certain disorders require early detection for effective treatment planning and ensuring a high quality of life for patients. Machine learning, employing both supervised and unsupervised algorithms, aids doctors in early disease diagnosis. By comparing new data to existing information on a particular ailment, ML raises red flags when symptoms warrant attention, enabling timely and appropriate action.

Improving Population Health

Machine learning utilizes patterns and trends in patient data to enhance population health. ML systems identify individuals at higher risk of developing chronic diseases, allowing for tailored treatments to curb disease spread.

Robot-Assisted Surgery

ML-powered surgical robots have revolutionized surgery by enhancing speed and accuracy. These systems perform complex surgical procedures with minimal blood loss, adverse effects, and discomfort. Noteworthy institutions, such as Maastricht University Medical Center, employ ML to enable surgical robots to stitch small blood arteries, demonstrating the technology's precision.

Enhancing Safety

ML can develop models predicting risks to patients, such as adverse drug interactions or postoperative complications, thereby reducing patient risks and enhancing the overall safety of medical treatments.

Supporting Clinical Research and Trials

Machine learning finds diverse applications in clinical trials and research, streamlining the participant selection process through predictive analytics. ML offers real-time monitoring and data access to trial participants, aids in determining optimal sample sizes, and eliminates data-based errors, potentially accelerating the pace and efficiency of clinical studies.

Drug Development

In the early stages of drug development, machine learning plays a crucial role, employing R&D technologies like next-generation sequencing and precision medicine. ML identifies patterns in data without making predictions, contributing to the discovery of alternative treatment paths for complex illnesses.

Explainable AI (XAI) in the Healthcare Sector

Explainable AI aims to enhance the transparency and interpretability of machine learning models. In healthcare, this involves providing clinicians with insights into the rationale behind specific decisions fostering trust and acceptance of AI-driven recommendations.

XAI techniques empower healthcare professionals to comprehend the underlying factors influencing an AI's diagnosis or treatment suggestion.

In critical healthcare applications like radiology and pathology, XAI is particularly significant. By elucidating their decisions, AI models can assist radiologists and pathologists in making more informed judgments, leading to heightened diagnostic accuracy and improved patient care.

Quantum Computing's Impact on Healthcare

Quantum computing holds substantial promise in addressing intricate healthcare challenges, including drug discovery, genomics, and the optimization of treatment plans. Traditional computers need help with the overwhelming computational complexity associated with these tasks. Quantum computers, however, can process vast datasets and execute intricate calculations at unprecedented speeds.

In genomics, quantum computing can expedite the analysis of extensive genomic datasets, aiding researchers in uncovering the genetic foundations of diseases and formulating personalized treatment strategies.

Furthermore, quantum computing can simulate molecular interactions with unparalleled accuracy, facilitating drug discovery and development.

Blockchain Integration in Healthcare Data Management

Blockchain technology has the potential to secure healthcare data, ensuring its integrity and granting patients greater control over their medical records. This decentralized approach can revolutionize data sharing in healthcare, allowing patients to authorize or revoke access to their medical records for trusted healthcare providers.

Additionally, blockchain can enhance the traceability of pharmaceuticals in the supply chain, mitigating the risk of counterfeit drugs entering the market. The immutability of blockchain guarantees that data will remain unalterable, bolstering the reliability of healthcare records and transactions.

Telemedicine and the Synergy with AI

The convergence of telemedicine and AI promises to broaden access to healthcare services, particularly in remote areas. AI-driven chatbots and virtual health assistants can furnish immediate medical advice, enhancing patient outcomes and alleviating the strain on healthcare facilities. AI-based telemedicine platforms can facilitate remote consultations, diagnoses, and patient monitoring.

Moreover, integrating telemedicine with AI-powered remote monitoring devices enables continuous health tracking. Wearable devices collect vital sign data, which AI algorithms analyze in real time. Healthcare providers receive alerts and insights, enabling prompt intervention when a patient's condition demands attention.

STEPS OF MACHINE LEARNING

Processing Steps

Step 1: Defining the Problem Statement

The defining of problem is the first step, where the purpose of studying the need to diagnose the heart disease is to be identified, i.e. the objective to predict the possibility of occurrence of heart disease in a patient. In this stage, it is also essential to consider the type of data that can be used.

Problem Definition

This stage outlines objectives and specific research questions. Identify sources, including primary and secondary data, such as surveys, interviews, databases, observation, experiments, and online platforms.

When planning for Data Collection, appropriate methods must be selected based on the nature of the data and research goals, such as surveys, interviews, observation, experiments, web scraping, and sensor data collection. First, we design data collection instruments, pilot the process to test tools and methods, and then proceed to collect data. Following this, we ensure accuracy and completeness during the data collection process. The common methods include:

  1. Surveys: Structured questionnaires administered to a target group to gather specific information.
  2. Interviews: Conducting one-on-one or group conversations to gain in-depth insights.
  3. Observation: Systematically observing and recording behaviors or events.
  4. Experiments: Controlling variables to study cause-and-effect relationships.
  5. Web scraping: Extracting data from websites and online sources.
  6. Sensor data collection: Gathering data from sensors or IoT devices.

Step 2: Data Gathering

In this step, the following things need to be discussed, such as:

  1. The selection of the dataset needed to solve this problem,
  2. The availability of the dataset,
  3. The source of the dataset.

As the data gathering is the most important step in the field of machine learning, hence the major finding is to select the dataset that is efficient, better and reliable. In our research work, we need to utilize the medical data, for the accurate prediction of diseases and hence, the dataset is searched from the various sources. The dataset that is selected by the various sources must be available for analyzing the predicted model. However, for learning by the machine learning technique, the data must be well-versed and collected only from the authenticated source, which had been used also in the previous research. Therefore, the dataset needed for our work must contain the basic details, like age, sex, blood sugar, etc., and should be used for further analysis [15].

Step 3: Data Preparation

It is the third step that is applied for the dataset being collected for the diagnosis of disease, the dataset is examined as it might be in the incorrect form and can have a lot of inconsistencies, such as missing values, redundant variables, duplicate values, etc. It is hence very essential to remove such inconsistencies; otherwise, it will lead to the wrong predictions and computations. Therefore, at this step, we scan the dataset and fix them.

Data Filtering

Data filtering involves selecting and presenting a specific subset of data based on predetermined criteria. The approach to filtering data can vary depending on the context, databases, spreadsheets, or programming languages.

To conduct effective data filtering, follow these steps:

Clearly Define Analysis Criteria

Precisely articulate the criteria you intend to analyze. For example, when evaluating revenue by customer, specify the relevant period and the customers for inclusion in the analysis.

Choose Appropriate Filtering Tools

Select suitable tools for data filtering based on your requirements. It may include SQL queries for database filtering or Excel filters for spreadsheet data, depending on the nature and source of your data.

Utilize SQL Queries

Construct SQL queries to filter data according to your defined criteria if working with databases. SQL provides robust filtering capabilities, enabling the extraction of specific data subsets for analysis.

Employ Excel Filters

In spreadsheet applications like Excel, leverage built-in filtering features to quickly sort and display data meeting specific criteria. It offers a swift and flexible means of analyzing information. Users can refine search criteria through an intuitive drop-down menu, streamlining data filtering for a personalized and efficient experience.

Specify Periods

When filtering data, consider time-related aspects. Specify relevant periods for your analysis to ensure accurate and meaningful insights.

Use Multiple Filters

Enhance your analysis by employing multiple filters simultaneously. For a comprehensive understanding, filter data based on factors like period, customer segment, and product type. This approach helps reveal detailed insights.

Explore Data Visualization

Leverage data visualization tools such as Tableau or Power BI to create visual representations of your filtered data. These tools facilitate an intuitive and comprehensive analysis, efficiently identifying trends, patterns, and outliers.

Iterate and Refine

The filtering process is often iterative. After an initial analysis, evaluate the results and consider refining your criteria or adjusting filters to gain deeper insights. This iterative approach ensures continuous improvement in the accuracy and relevance of your analysis.

Step 4: Data Analysis

In this step, deep diving to find the hidden information in the dataset is performed. The Exploratory Data Analysis or EDA is the brainstorming stage of machine learning, and the data exploration provides an understanding of the patterns and trends in the data. This step is therefore used to view all the insights and to find the correlations between the variables defined. As in our research work, we need to focus that whether there is a possibility of heart disease in a patient that can be diagnosed beforehand.

Removal of Missing Values

It is now time to handle the missing values present in the data. One way to handle the missing values in the data would be to just remove those rows as explained earlier. Assuming that we are using python, which is the default language used by many data scientists for machine learning applications, let us also see the code at which this could be done.

Imputation

It is the process of substituting the missing values with various imputing strategies such as mean, median, and mode imputation. However, imputation can be done randomly by assigning values to the data based on the domain knowledge as well. It is also important to note that imputation can also be performed based on the machine learning predictions from all the remaining features that already contain no missing values. In this way, the model learns to find patterns and make predictions for the unknown values in the feature, respectively.

Outliers

Datasets often contain outliers or data points whose values are quite far from what was expected in our data. This can be due to human error when recording the values or faulty machines that record features. When we are trying to evaluate the metrics for machine learning with some being the mean squared error, the presence of an outlier in the data could significantly increase the error. But this does not give us the most accurate picture of our model performance. Furthermore, there are many machine learning models that are not robust to outliers in the data. Therefore, steps must be taken to remove them in the data processing stage so that we get a true representation of our model when using metrics such as the mean squared error along with ensuring that models generate the best predictions without being suspectable to outliers.

Transforming the Data

After filling in the missing values along with removing the outliers, the next step would be to transform this data so that it becomes feasible to train on the machine learning models. There are many ways to transform the data depending on the type of data and the business requirements.

Dimensionality Reduction

One of the setbacks of having a high-dimensionality data (higher number of features) is that there is a phenomenon called “curse of dimensionality”, where increased features have diminishing returns. Therefore, it is important to remove those features that do not have a significant impact on the model predictions and the output. Reducing the dimensions does two things: it reduces the time it takes for the machine learning model to get trained on the data and it can also sometimes remove outliers from data. Hence, we should be performing dimensionality reduction to ensure that we get a more robust model after training it.

There are various ways in which higher dimensional data is reduced to a lower dimensional representation. There are techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Stochastic Neighborhood embedding (t-SNE), and UMAPs, which could be used to reduce dimensionality. Note that each of these methods works differently under the hood but the product is to reduce the dimensions.

Standardization

It is also a good practice to standardize the data and ensure that all the input features are on the same scale before giving them to the machine learning models. Consider an example of two features: height and weight. Let us consider that the output variable that we are going to be predicting with ML algorithms is “outdoor activity”. We know that height can be measured in centimeters (cm) while weight is measured in kilograms (kg). We usually cannot compare these two features as they are not on the same scale. But if we were to convert these features such that they represent the same scale, this ensures that we might compare them and decide which feature was the most influential in determining the “outdoor activity” of a person.

Normalization

Data that is present in a different scale can be problematic as we have seen in the above case. There is also an alternate strategy to deal with data that is present in different scales. One way is to normalize the data which means that we are subtracting the present value from the minimum value in a particular feature, and we divide the result with the difference between the maximum value and the minimum value in the feature of interest. This is also an effective way to transform the data. Below is the equation about how this is done to get a good idea.

Based on the equation, let us understand the values present which are given.

  • Xmin = The minimum value present in the feature
  • Xmax = The maximum value present in the feature
  • Xnorm = The normalized value obtained because of performing this operation.
Binning

It is important to address the outliers present in the data that impact the performance of machine learning models. One of the ways to reduce the impact of these outliers is to divide the data points into various bins based on an important feature. In other words, it is sorting the wide data set into smaller groups of more similar data. This ensures that the outliers in the data have a minimal impact overall on the predictions. Therefore, this is also an effective way to transform the data.

Clustering

Whenever we are dealing with unsupervised machine learning where the output or the target variable is not known, one of the popular approaches with this data is clustering. While clustering can be used for unsupervised machine learning, it can also be used for supervised machine learning as well. If we were to cluster the data based on a particular feature, we could form groups of the data that we have considered. The data could also be transformed because of this approach, and we are better able to find patterns in it.

Step 5: Building A Model

Finally, the model is built, by using all the patterns and insights derived during the previous phase of data exploration. In this stage of machine learning, the dataset is split into two parts i.e. in the training and the testing data. The training data is used to build and analyze the model. The logic of the model is built on the algorithm of machine learning that is being implemented. The right algorithm that is to be chosen must be dependent on the type of problem, the data set, and the level of complexity of the problem that is to be solved. Since in our work, the output is in the form of true or false, therefore a classification algorithm such as Logistic Regression can be used.

Step 6: Model Evaluation Optimization

After building a model by using the training data set, the model is finally tested. The testing is performed on the dataset to check the efficiency of the model, and its ability to predict the accuracy, and once the accuracy is calculated, any further improvements in the model can be implemented at this stage by using methods like parameter tuning and cross-validation to improve the performance of the model.

Step 7: Predictions

Once the model is evaluated and improved, it is finally used to predict whether it is giving the correct predictions about the disease. The final output depicts the current scope of using the techniques and gives us accurate predictions by using machine learning techniques.

FUTURE SCOPE

The future scope of data collection and preparation for medical applications in machine learning holds immense promise for revolutionizing healthcare. The convergence of diverse and expansive datasets, ranging from electronic health records and medical imaging to genomics and wearable devices, is poised to offer a comprehensive understanding of individual health. Ensuring the quality and standardization of this data is imperative for training robust and generalizable machine learning models. Privacy and ethical considerations loom large, necessitating advanced anonymization techniques and adherence to stringent data protection regulations. Real-time data integration, particularly from IoT sensors and wearable devices, will provide a dynamic and continuous stream of health updates, enabling timely interventions. The future also demands machine learning models that are accurate but also explainable and interpretable, fostering trust among healthcare professionals and patients. The evolution toward federated learning, which allows model training without centralizing raw data, addresses concerns related to data privacy. Integration into clinical workflows, continuous monitoring, collaboration, and compliance with regulatory frameworks are pivotal for successfully deploying machine learning in medical applications. As the field advances, open data initiatives, and interdisciplinary partnerships will further acc- elerate progress, ensuring that machine learning becomes an integral and transformative force in healthcare.

CONCLUSION

In conclusion, the exploration of data collection and preparation for medical applications in Machine Learning (ML) within the healthcare domain underscores the critical role that high-quality, well-curated data plays in the success of ML models. This chapter has delved into the complexities and nuances of acquiring, processing, and organizing medical data, recognizing it as the foundational building block for practical ML applications.

The challenges associated with data collection in healthcare, including privacy, security, and interoperability issues, are substantial but not insurmountable. The continual advancement of data standards, ethical considerations, and regulatory frameworks is paramount to overcoming these challenges. As the healthcare industry becomes increasingly data-driven, establishing a robust infrastructure for collecting and preparing diverse datasets is essential.

The future of ML in healthcare hinges on our ability to enhance data collection methodologies, ensuring inclusivity, accuracy, and representativeness across diverse populations. Moreover, ongoing data standardization and interoperability efforts will be pivotal in creating a seamless flow of information, fostering collaboration, and enabling the development of more powerful and generalized ML models.

This chapter serves as a guide, emphasizing the importance of meticulous data collection and preparation processes as the cornerstone for successful ML applications in healthcare. It calls for a collaborative approach involving healthcare professionals, data scientists, policymakers, and technology experts to navigate the complexities and ensure that the data used in ML models is comprehensive, ethically sourced, and responsibly handled. As we move forward, the commitment to refining data collection practices will undoubtedly contribute to the evolution of healthcare, paving the way for more accurate diagnostics, personalized treatment plans, and improved patient outcomes.

Growing Importance of Machine Learning in Healthcare to Determine Potential Risk



Suchismita Mishra1, *
1 Inderprastha Engineering College, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh 201010, India

Abstract

The growing convenience of electronic healthcare data represents a significant opportunity within the healthcare segment, offering the potential for both pioneering discoveries as well as practical applications aimed at improving the overall quality of healthcare. Nevertheless, for healthcare epidemiologists to fully harness the potential of all these data, there is a pursuing need for computational techniques capable of handling extensive and intricate datasets. Machine learning (ML), which involves the investigation of tools and methodologies for discovering hidden patterns within data, develops as a valuable resource in this context. The cautious implementation of Machine Learning techniques with electronic healthcare data embraces the potential of a comprehensive transformation of patient risk assessment, traversing across the entire spectrum of medical disciplines and predominantly impacting the domain of infectious diseases. Such a transformation could ultimately lead to the development of precise interventions designed to mitigate the proliferation of healthcare-associated pathogens. Healthcare epidemiologists are facing an increasingly demanding task of processing and deciphering extensive and intricate datasets. This challenge arises in the cycle with the expanding role of healthcare epidemiologists, paralleled by the growing prevalence of electronic health data. The availability of substantial volumes of high-quality data at both the patient and facility levels has opened new avenues for exploration. Specifically, these data hold the potential to enhance our comprehension of the risk factors associated with healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), refine patient risk assessment methodologies, and unveil the pathways responsible for the intra- and interfacility transmission of infectious diseases. These insights, in turn, pave the way for targeted preventive measures.

Historically, a significant portion of clinical data remained unutilized, often due to the sheer magnitude and intricacy of the data itself, as well as the absence of suitable techniques for data collection and storage. These valuable data resources were frequently underappreciated and underutilized. However, the advent of novel and improved data collection and storage methods, such as electronic health records, has presented a unique opportunity to address this issue. Especially, machine learning has begun to permeate the realm of clinical literature at large. The prudent application of

Machine Learning within the domain of healthcare epidemiology (HE) holds the promise of yielding substantial returns on the considerable investments made in data collection within the field. In the context of this research work, the initiative has been given by elucidating the fundamental principles of Machine Learning, subsequently investigating its relevance and applications within the realm of healthcare epidemiology, reinforced by illustrative instances of successful research endeavours.

Finally, we outline some of the reasonable considerations essential for the design and execution of ML methodologies within the field of healthcare epidemiology. Within the scope of this research, an effort has been initiated by providing an introductory overview of the fundamental principles of Machine Learning.

Subsequently, it is explored into an exploration of how Machine Learning stands poised to revolutionize healthcare epidemiology, substantiating our discussion with illustrative instances of successful applications.

Keywords: Clinical data, Data-driven computation, Healthcare epidemiologist, Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), Machine learning, Patient risk stratification.

INTRODUCTION

The term “Machine Learning (ML)” encompasses assorted numerical methodologies enabling computers to learn from experience without explicit programming. Such kind of learning manifests as alterations in algorithmic functionality, demonstrated by an ML system discerning faces through analysis of a myriad of photographs depicting diverse individuals. The two primary branches of ML, i.e. unsupervised and supervised learning, strengthen its multifaceted applications. Within the expansive realm of healthcare, a pivotal industry globally, the integration of ML technology emerges as a transformative force, promising a renaissance analogous to the substantial advancements witnessed in the past century.

The healthcare sector, frequently at the forefront of adopting cutting-edge technologies, has seamlessly integrated Artificial Intelligence (AI) and ML, mirroring their universal influence in business and e-commerce. ML, operating at the intersection of computational prowess and healthcare imperatives, has already demonstrated its value through the utilization of Big Data tools in data analytics, particularly in the context of Electronic Medical Records (EMR). Beyond this, ML's trajectory holds a great promise for future implementation, accentuating its role in enhancing the worth of automation as well as the intelligent process of decision-making within primary and tertiary patient care along with public healthcare systems.

In the context of the clinical trial research, machine learning technologies arise as indispensable tools. The application of refined predictive analytics to assess clinical trials of these applicants enables medical specialists to navigate massive data arrays, leading to reduced costs and time associated with medical tests. ML applications further contribute to enhancing clinical trial efficiency by assisting in the determination of optimum sample size, thereby boosting efficacy along with minimizing the potential for data errors, particularly over the integration of Electronic Health Records.

ML's impact extends to addressing challenges in the insufficiency of well-trained radiologists globally. Through ML algorithms, the healthcare industry gains the capability of dealing with individualized therapies that are both dynamic and efficient, leveraging personal health data and predictive analytics. The potential for ML in research and clinical trials is immense, facilitating the identification of latent trial participants through predictive research based on assorted data points such as previous medical interactions and social media activities. Real-time observation of trial participants, coupled with electronic record utilization, further enhances the precision and efficiency of clinical trials, with the overarching aim of optimizing sample sizes and minimizing data-related errors.

The significant potential of ML in healthcare encompasses a gamut of applications, ranging from the refinement of patient care and public health systems to the optimization of clinical trials and research endeavors. The integration of ML technologies not only reflects the evolution of healthcare practices but also holds the promise of substantially improving the quality of life for a global population.

NECESSITY OF MACHINE LEARNING IN HEALTHCARE

The uninterrupted enhancement of healthcare services and the evolving capacity to address complex diseases are indisputable progressions. However, persistent challenges, particularly in determining optimal dosages and treatment durations for individuals or patient groups with some degree of clinical studies, such as children, underscore the need for innovative solutions. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as a successful integration into pediatric care, offering the capability to predict personalized and optimal treatments for children [1, 2].

The advent of COVID-19 pandemic has propelled ML to the forefront of organizational strategies seeking competitive advantages in an environment marked by volatility and improbability. From operational streamlining to catalysing Research and Development (R&D), ML has contributed to assisting hospitals and health systems in navigating unique challenges. ML technology, a dynamic subset of Artificial Intelligence (AI), stands as a focal point for numerous companies striving to harness its potential across diverse domains, from business to healthcare [3].

The escalating popularity of ML is rooted in its utilization of algorithms to facilitate data-driven learning, presenting adaptable applications in the ever-evolving landscape of healthcare. The healthcare sector undergoes eternal transformation driven by advancements in technology and ideas. ML emerges as a valuable tool in addressing novel scenarios within healthcare, vesting medical professionals with insights derived from algorithms capable of processing unstructured text a task historically challenging on a large scale. This invasion of ML-derived intelligence equips physicians and administrators with the means to make well-informed decisions promptly, impacting patient care and operational programs that have far-reaching consequences for millions of lives. The convergence of ML and healthcare is to redesign paradigms and enhance the efficiency of healthcare systems, marking a significant stride in the journey toward improved patient outcomes and operational excellence.

PILLARS OF MACHINE LEARNING IN THE HEALTHCARE SECTOR

The application of Machine Learning (ML) within the healthcare domain is a subject of extensive examination due to its diverse and impactful capabilities. Various enablers and quality pillars play a crucial role in enhancing the support and care provided by healthcare units. Especially, the ML concept contributes significantly to several aspects, including outbreak prediction, medical imaging diagnosis, behavioral modifications, and the meticulous management of patient data. These quality pillars illuminate the robust foundation upon which ML operates, delivering effective and unquestionable performance in addressing the requirements of healthcare practices.

The illustrated efficacy of these ML attributes establishes them as essential components, particularly when such services are domineering within healthcare contexts. The multifaceted contributions of ML, spanning from predicting outbreaks to improving medical imaging and patient data management, exemplify its potential to advance healthcare services for the greater benefit of society. The intrinsic qualities and performance metrics of ML in these domains underscore its indispensability in supporting and enhancing various facets of healthcare delivery.

Machine Learning (ML) represents a process wherein computers are refined to distinguish patterns through the provision of data and algorithmic frameworks [4]. The manual detection of diseases stances significant challenges, prompting ML to assume a pivotal role in diagnosing sicknesses, monitoring patient health, and recommending preventive measures. This extends from addressing minor illnesses to tackling formidable conditions like early-stage cancer detection. Notably, ML applications have demonstrated efficacy in global mental health predictions, aiding clinicians in identifying demographic segments vulnerable to stressors such as pandemics or natural disasters. Moreover, ML's capabilities incorporate assessing biological features and optimizing molecule selection based on the desired biological activity and physicochemical attributes.

The integration of crowdsourcing into the medical domain has emerged as a contemporary approach, enabling access to extensive datasets contributed by individuals with their consent. Real-time health data, incorporated from sources such as social media inputs, information from satellites, websites, and records kept in institutions, undergoes analysis through ML-driven networks. This analytical expertise proves instrumental in forecasting diverse health phenomena, from various infectious diseases outbreaks. ML's role in streamlining the time-consuming and costly process of updating and maintaining health data is crucial, offering a potential avenue for significant time, cost, and effort savings.

ML's transformative potential in healthcare extends to a shift from a responsive to a preventive approach by delivering individualized treatment recommendations [5]. In clinical applications, ML aids clinicians in tailoring therapies based on exclusive traits of a patient with critical symptoms, thereby reducing the prospect of contrary impacts from prescription medications. ML algorithms contribute to predicting and tracking disease outbreaks, mitigating poor epidemic outcomes, and simplifying the drug detection process along with clinical experiments. The technology's ability to monitor and evaluate vast amounts of data ensures the safety and efficacy of medications.

The inherent learning capabilities of ML models, operating through numerous learning methods like supervised and unsupervised methods, enable the generation of prescriptive and predictive insights. Beyond diagnostics, ML enhances patient concern and revival by facilitating on-time alarms and announcements related to appointments, collection of the report, and related activities. Notably, ML applications excel in disease identification and diagnosis, particularly in cases involving inherited and genetic issues or some specific categories of cancer disease, still challenging to detect in their initial stages.

The machine learning application in the field of healthcare addresses a range of challenges, enhancing the quality of life for patients and optimizing resource utilization within the healthcare system [6]. The advent of a value-based approach to cancer care underscores the significance of access to linkable health data and collaboration among diverse stakeholders. ML significantly contributes to organizational and administrative aspects of healthcare delivery, automating tasks and record administration. This automation potential not only saves time but also eradicates the need for manual interventions in various healthcare processes.

ML emerges as a proactive tool in identifying and addressing health issues before symptoms apparent, particularly in cases like diabetes where early detection is critical [7]. ML models can separate subtle, subconscious actions, prompting essential lifestyle modifications. This ranges from wearables encouraging movement after prolonged inactivity to applications guiding posture adjustments. ML's role in the rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines showcases the effectiveness of data-driven methodologies. The integration of image recognition algorithms enhances radiology diagnosis, while diverse datasets from social media to wearable medical records contribute to forecasting health issues. The reduction of false positives and false negatives in various applications, such as sensor alarms, emphasizes ML's role in refining diagnostic accuracy.

ML has become an integral part of diverse industries, driving progressions in telemedicine, self-driving cars, hyper-targeted ads, and other solutions that enhance business profitability and customer-centricity [8]. In healthcare, ML empowers professionals with tools and techniques that significantly impact health outcomes. Intelligent predictive algorithms in ML software offer immediate benefits in disciplines with extensive datasets. The tailored recommendation of physical activities based on individual profiles highlights ML's role in promoting precautionary health practices. The continuous interaction of self-trained ML systems with clinical study data highlights the symbiotic relationship between human activity and ML. Finally, the finance and banking sector, rich in structured data, stands as an ideal field for AI and ML applications, contributing to unparalleled advancements and enhanced experiences for practitioners and clients alike.

APPLICATIONS OF MACHINE LEARNING IN HEALTHCARE

Healthcare organizations can influence ML to enhance risk adjustment, employing algorithms that efficiently extract information from clinical charts, surpassing manual review processes in speed and accuracy. These ML technologies become more intelligent with increased document processing, enabling plans and providers to uncover concealed risk factors and healthcare gaps, thereby refining risk score accuracy. ML empowers the healthcare profession to manage risk effectively and enhance patient care quality by identifying and addressing gaps in care. This technology, rooted in algorithmic mechanisms, acquires a set of instructions to execute specific tasks, allowing medical professionals to absorb pertinent data unconventionally. The reliability and effectiveness of data analysis through ML tools in healthcare have heightened, fostering prospects for accelerated diagnosis and improved patient recovery in evolving healthcare services.

ML applications in healthcare encompass algorithms fortified with self-learning neural networks, elevating treatment quality by assessing external data sources such as a patient's condition, X-rays, CT scans, and various tests and screenings.

Out there patient care, the deployment of ML in healthcare enhances organizational efficiency. ML technologies regulate processes like claims processing and revenue cycle management, with the potential for automating clinical documentation and records administration. Corporate use cases are continually developing, underscoring the significant potential and advancements ML could bring to the healthcare industry. Notably, algorithms have shown superior performance to radiologists in detecting malignant tumours [114].

In medical sector research and development, ML offers several promising applications. Recognizing the considerable expenses and time speculation associated with clinical trials in the pharmaceutical industry, ML-based predictive analytics prove irreplaceable. By identifying potential clinical trials using a wide array of data points, including previous doctor visits and social media interactions, researchers can efficiently create trial participant pools. ML contributes to real-time monitoring and data access for trial participants, determines optimal sample sizes, and utilizes electronic records to minimize data-related errors. An ML-based approach to identifying toxic compounds before entering clinical trials holds the potential for substantial cost savings [115].

ANALYSIS OF THE IMPACT OF MACHINE LEARNING ON HEALTH CARE

In the up-to-date landscape of the healthcare industry, machine learning (ML) has become universal, exerting a substantial influence on diverse domains, including self-driving cars, speech recognition, and remarkably, medical research and treatment. Researchers are actively leveraging ML algorithms to pioneer early cancer detection, discerning biomarkers in the blood associated with various cancers. The application of ML extends essentially to laboratory diagnostics, image and cycle management, intelligent clinical data analysis, and computer-aided medical procedures like organ recognition and tissue characterization.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into smartphone apps simplifies improved inpatient treatment and diagnosis, with machines proficiently interpreting CT scans and other diagnostic imaging tools for the identification of abnormalities. The trajectory of ML's impact extends to consumer health applications, anticipating further integration into endeavors that enhance patients' health experiences beyond hospital confines, including the identification of high-risk patients within populations.

Beyond healthcare, ML advancements are driving accurate predictions, effective asset management, and in-depth market analysis transversely various industries. Intelligent chatbots, designed with ML capabilities, are enhancing response management and customer service in the corporate realm, particularly within marketing firms.

The healthcare industry has experienced a paradigm shift with the integration of ML, nurturing improvements in care quality and patient outcomes across diagnostics and drug discovery. ML automation is addressing the challenges posed by the exponential growth of data, encompassing health records, clinical trials, and claims processing, and billing records, offering valuable insights for informed decision-making by healthcare professionals.

ML is transforming patient care strategies and healthcare delivery systems through techniques such as natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. Deep learning algorithms, rooted in ML, empower accurate and efficient automated diagnostic suggestions, resulting in cost reductions, administrative relief, and expedited reporting of vital cases. Prescriptions are benefiting from ML's ability to reduce errors and enhance diagnostic speed, leveraging diagnostic results and audits.

Healthcare professionals, equipped with an understanding of ML opportunities, can cooperate to enhance clinical outcomes and streamline hospital experiences. The transformative impact of ML extends to hospital management, medical decision support, and the customization of treatment plans, optimizing outcomes for patients. Additionally, ML contributes to patient education by demonstrating key outcomes and disease trials, thereby improving overall health systems and hospital management efficiency while reducing costs.

Incorporating object detection and image recognition, ML contributes to computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for disease detection and prediction. Deep learning models provide practical clarifications of imaging data, offering insights into tissue shape, size, and volume. ML's progress has led to improved handling of patient data and records, the development of novel medical procedures, and more effective approaches to treating chronic diseases.

As the volume of available data continues to escalate, ML's integration with data and analytics is set to redefine how healthcare applications store, share, and utilize information. Nevertheless, challenges persist, with difficulties such as acquiring patient data sets of requisite quality and quantity, navigating privacy and security restrictions, and addressing data format and quality issues representing barriers to the seamless incorporation of ML in healthcare.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

Machine Learning (ML) stands as a potent tool for doctors, scientists, and researchers, marking a continuous stream of breakthroughs and succeeding applications in healthcare. The relentless advancement of ML has garnered attention from the medical industry, introducing concepts that contribute significantly to patient care, disease detection, proactive management, patient engagement, and more. Across the globe, healthcare organizations leverage AI-driven resolutions and ML models to enhance service delivery and expedite the development of treatments for critical ailments. Virtual clinical trials, sequencing, and pattern identification are now accelerated processes, facilitated by ML technologies.

The integration of smart medical devices is making technology-enabled healthcare a reality, offering promising prospects for the future of ML in the healthcare sector. ML's capacity to process diverse data points, accurately predict risks and outcomes and execute various tasks positions it as a tool for creating personalized prescriptions tailored to individuals' exclusive needs. As the healthcare industry embraces innovation, ML is expected to play a pivotal role in medicine delivery, potentially in collaboration with nanotechnology.

ML addresses current healthcare challenges and anticipates future issues, playing a crucial role in forecasting global outbreaks. It sifts through vast amounts of data, including website data and real-time social media updates, to verify information and forecast occurrences from communal illnesses to severe infectious diseases.

In the realm of scientific research, ML's occurrence is increasing, demonstrating its implication in processing large datasets, making accurate predictions, and aiding scientists in more efficient discovery. ML's application in epidemiological studies holds the ability for the future of precision medicine, particularly when paired with individual health considerations. The predictive analytics component of ML becomes instrumental in tailoring treatments to individual patients, generating numerous therapy alternatives based on patient’s medical history.

As ML continues to develop, there is a growing need for medical education to incorporate coursework on ML and its applications. Medical students, residents, and fellows should be equipped with knowledge of ML and data science during their training, ensuring that they are well-versed in leveraging these technologies for improved patient care and medical research.

Challenges and Opportunities for the Healthcare



Prateek Jain1, *, Rachna Behl1, Abhishek Saxena2, Rohit Bathla1
1 Manav Rachna International Institute of Research & Studies, Faridabad, Haryana, India
2 Manav Rachna University, Faridabad, Haryana, India

Abstract

Machine learning technology is a rapidly growing field aiming to create systems replicating human intelligence. In the healthcare sector, machine learning is not meant to replace human physicians but to provide better solutions to healthcare problems. It plays a critical role in the development of automated computational approaches. It has numerous applications in radiology, computer-aided drug design, virtual health assistance, clinical decisions, disease outbreaks, healthcare management, and administration. Security and privacy risks are a significant concern with AI-powered healthcare systems since the healthcare sector has distinct security and privacy requirements to safeguard patients' medical information. Despite this, using machine learning in healthcare has many benefits, including faster analysis of large datasets, improved safety of clinical trials, better insights into predictive screening, higher accuracy, reduced healthcare costs, and increased efficiency. Although many AI and machine learning applications have been successfully deployed in medical research and continue to deliver favorable results, challenges still need to be addressed. In this book chapter, we delve into the latest challenges and opportunities that the healthcare industry faces. We explore the changing landscape of healthcare and provide insights into how technological advancements, regulatory changes, and shifting patient expectations are shaping the future of healthcare delivery. Whether you're a healthcare professional, policymaker, or just interested in the industry, this chapter will provide valuable insights and a fresh perspective on the challenges and opportunities faced by the healthcare industry today.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Healthcare, Machine learning.

INTRODUCTION

Artificial Intelligence

There is a growing assertion that Artificial Intelligence is taking on a more significant role in educational technology, management sciences, and operational

research. Intelligence is the capacity to acquire information for addressing intricate challenges and it will supplant human capabilities across various domains.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a specialized field within the realm of computer science dedicated to crafting innovative computer systems. These Intelligent Systems aim to mimic human-like intelligence, enabling the development of systems capable of human-like reasoning. AI finds its use in various applications such as robotics, expert systems, computerized translation tools, speech recognition, natural language statements, audio investigation, simulations, and theorems for problem-solving [1].

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the capability of an artificial entity to tackle complex problems by utilising its intelligence. Intelligence refers to the computational aspect of an entity's ability to achieve real-world objectives. It encompasses the capacity to think, visualise, remember, understand, recognise patterns, make decisions, adapt to changes, and learn from experience. AI focuses on making computers exhibit more human-like behaviour and achieving this in a fraction of the time it would take a human, which is termed artificial intelligence. AI is concerned with forcing the boundaries of practical computer science, striving to produce universal, adaptable, and competent systems of autonomously acquiring studies and solution strategies by applying general knowledge to specific situations.

Popular perception often associates AI with robots and self-driving cars. However, this perspective needs to pay attention to one of the Artificial Intelligence's most crucial and practical applications: analysing vast amounts of daily data. AI can help us achieve exceptional speed and scalability in gathering insights and automating processes if applied strategically. Fig. (1) displays the interrelated fields of AI.

Fig. (1))
Fields of AI.

Types of Artificial Intelligence

Based on Capabilities

Narrow Artificial Intelligence

Narrow Artificial Intelligence, also known as “weak Artificial Intelligence,” is specialised in performing specific tasks with intelligence. It is the most prevalent and currently accessible form. The training for this Artificial Intelligence is given exclusively for a single task, and its operation lies within the predefined boundaries of that specific task. Consequently, when it encounters situations beyond its designated domain, it may exhibit unexpected failures. Apple's Siri is a prime illustration of Narrow Artificial Intelligence, albeit its capabilities are limited to specific functions. Forexample: providing product recommendations on an e-commerce platform, enabling, and identifying images.

General Artificial Intelligence

General Artificial Intelligence is more advanced than Narrow Artificial Intelligence because it can handle various tasks and adapt to new challenges. It can understand, learn, and apply knowledge in multiple domains like humans. It can switch tasks, learn, reason, and apply knowledge, exhibiting flexibility and adaptability. It can understand and engage in natural language, solve complex problems, and surpass Narrow AI. Despite its tremendous potential, achieving General AI remains a problematic and ongoing challenge. AI systems are designed to have the same breadth and depth of intelligence as humans.

Based on Functionalities

Reactive Machines

Purely reactive machines represent the most fundamental form of Artificial Intelligence.

These AI systems cannot retain past experiences or memories for future decision-making. Instead, they concentrate solely on the current situation and respond based on the best possible course of action, e.g., IBM's Deep Blue system and Google's AlphaGo.

Limited Memory

Machines with limited memory possess the capacity to retain past experiences or specific data temporarily, but this storage is time-restricted. They can make use of this stored information for a finite duration. For example, self-driving cars can save data like nearby cars' speeds, distances to other vehicles, speed limits, etc. A summary of different types is presented in Fig. (2).

Fig. (2))
Types of artificial intelligence.

MACHINE LEARNING

Machine learning is a process that empowers machines to acquire knowledge autonomously, eliminating the need for manual programming. Its primary focus involves employing sophisticated algorithms and statistical methods to analyze data and make predictions instead of relying on rule-based systems. The dataset plays a pivotal role in enhancing the accuracy of machine learning predictions, ensuring that the data is pertinent, and the forecasts are precise. Machine learning finds applications in various sectors like finance, retail, and healthcare [2].

The concept of machine learning (ML) has attracted considerable attention in recent years, primarily driven by the significant increase in data generation within the healthcare sector. According to a report (source not provided), approximately 86% of healthcare institutions have embraced various ML solutions, and over 80% of healthcare executives have devised plans involving artificial intelligence (AI) [3]. Machine learning, a critical component of the broader field of artificial intelligence, is defined as the ability of a machine to mimic intelligent human behavior. An algorithm learns from data and makes decisions based on similarities in new data [4].

It is essential to highlight that the collaboration of diverse fields, including mathematics, statistics, and computer science, is central to the data science framework necessary to implement various Machine Learning (ML) models [5]. While human intelligence is impressive, it has limitations due to errors caused by short-term memory [6]. However, with the increasing amount of data and the growing capability of computers to process and utilize this data to create a variety of machine learning algorithms, ML can help humans make better decisions by incorporating a significant amount of contextual information.

ML has found numerous medical applications, such as heart failure management, clinical decision support, and medical imaging.

Machine learning symbolizes a dynamic and transformative field at the intersections of computer science, AI, and data analysis. Over recent years, it has surged in significance as a technology-driven paradigm that empowers machines to acquire knowledge and enhance their performance autonomously, eliminating the need for explicit programming. Machine learning works because computers can learn from data, discern patterns, and make data-informed decisions, mirroring how humans gain expertise through experience. This capacity has given rise to revolutionary advancements spanning many sectors, including healthcare, finance, autonomous vehicle technology, and natural language processing, fundamentally altering our approach to solving complex problems and making predictions.

Need for Machine Learning

The significance of machine learning is driven by the exponential growth in data volumes and diversity, the increased accessibility and affordability of computational power, and the widespread availability of high-speed Internet. These factors of digital transformation enable the rapid and automated development of models capable of efficiently and accurately analyzing enormous and intricate datasets. It offers many applications for cost reduction, risk mitigation, and overall improvement in the quality of life. These applications span recommending products/services, detecting cybersecurity breaches, and facilitating the implementation of self-driving cars. With an expanding pool of accessible data and enhanced computational capabilities, machine learning is progressively becoming an integral part of daily life, poised to be seamlessly integrated into various aspects of human existence.

Advantages of Machine Learning in Healthcare

This technology offers a diverse array of applications for enhancing the realm of healthcare research. ML is helpful in various applications, from early disease detection to reduced healthcare costs. By using advanced predictive analytics to evaluate individuals participating in clinical trials, healthcare professionals can examine broader data, ultimately decreasing the expenses and time required for medical assessments. Several machine learning applications are poised to enhance the effectiveness of clinical trials even further, including determining ideal sample sizes for improved efficacy and mitigating data errors by utilizing Electronic Health Records (EHRs).

Healthcare institutions have harnessed the power of machine learning systems to proactively monitor and predict potential epidemic outbreaks across diverse regions of the world. This digital system effectively predicts disease outbreaks by gathering satellite data, real-time social media updates, and other essential online information sources. Its potential benefits are particularly significant in under-resourced third-world countries that require more healthcare infrastructure. Machine learning and data-driven techniques directly address issues such as lengthy queues, the fear of overwhelming medical bills, complex appointment processes, and difficulties accessing the right healthcare provider. These long-standing problems have plagued conventional healthcare systems for decades, but machine learning techniques are already vital to the solution. This is primarily due to the prowess of machine learning systems, which leverage vast databases and intelligent search algorithms to excel in tasks involving pattern recognition and optimization challenges. Another valuable aspect of machine learning in the healthcare sector is its ability to provide personalized and dynamically efficient therapies by integrating individual health data with predictive analytics.

In recent years, the widespread accessibility of hardware and cloud computing has ushered in an expanded use of machine learning (ML) across various facets of human life. The healthcare sector, too, has embraced this technological evolution. ML algorithms within healthcare hold immense promise, primarily owing to the wealth of data collected for each patient. These algorithms also excel in planning and offering comprehensive treatment recommendations to patients, resulting in reduced costs and an improved patient experience. Machine learning, therefore, emerges as a hidden gem for the healthcare industry. Within the vast reservoirs of unstructured data contained in patient records, historical treatments, and the medical history of the patient's family, ML aids healthcare professionals in anticipating genuine health issues by analyzing patients' historical data.

AI-powered tools have numerous advantages over traditional diagnostic methods. They are more precise, cost-effective, and save time. Additionally, AI can reduce the chances of human errors and provide accurate results in a shorter period. AI technology can enhance medical decision-making by offering real-time insights and support to healthcare providers. Ongoing research explores various AI applications in healthcare, including medical diagnosis and treatment, personalized medicine, drug discovery and development, genomic analysis, clinical decision support, and more.

However, it is essential to recognize that implementing ML in healthcare poses several challenges. These challenges include data privacy and security concerns, ethical considerations, and the need for robust validation and regulatory oversight to ensure the safety and effectiveness of these technologies.

Machine Learning and its Models

There are two categories of machine learning: supervised and unsupervised, as illustrated in Fig. (3). In supervised machine learning, algorithms are trained using established input and output data to predict future outcomes. On the other hand, unsupervised machine learning aims to discover hidden patterns or inherent structures within the input data. Supervised machine learning is suitable for classification and regression tasks, while unsupervised machine learning is primarily used for clustering tasks [7] as shown in Table 2.

Fig. (3))
Classification of machine learning.

Supervised Classification Machine Learning Algorithms

Supervised learning is machine learning with labelled data. The training data works as a supervisor to teach the machine to predict the output correctly. It is a process of providing the input and correct output data to the machine learning model. Hence, its algorithms aim to find a mapping function to map the input variable(x) with the output variable(y). The primary goal of the predictive or supervised learning approach is to learn a mapping from inputs x to outputs y, with a given labelled set of input-output pairs.

D = {(xi, yi)} N with i=1.

D is the training set, and N is the number of training examples.

In simple terms, each training input xi is a D dimensional vector of numbers called the features, attributes, or covariates. Similarly, the form of the output or the response variable can be anything, but many methods consider that yi is a categorical or nominal variable from some finite set, yi Ɛ {1... C} or yi is a real-valued scalar. Hence, when yi is unequivocal, the problem is known as the classification or pattern recognition, and when it is real valued, the problem is known as regression.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Supervised Learning

  1. Supervised learning uses labelled datasets, which makes it highly accurate in predicting object classes.
  2. This type of learning allows algorithms to predict outputs based on prior experience.
  3. Supervised learning algorithms may struggle with solving complex tasks.
  4. Training the algorithm can be time-consuming due to the high computational requirements Table 1.
